messages.content:
# MILP Model for Conflict Detection and Resolution in Railway Traffic Management

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $S$ | Set of block sections (track-side detection sections), indexed by $s$ |
| $S^{SW} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections |
| $S \setminus S^{SW}$ | Open-line and platform sections |
| $P_i$ | Set of speed profile options for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i = (s_{i,1}, s_{i,2}, \ldots, s_{i,n_i})$ | Ordered route (sequence of sections) for train $i$ |
| $R_i(k)$ | The $k$-th section on train $i$'s route |
| $\mathcal{C}_s = \{(i,j) : i, j \in I, \, i \neq j, \, s \in R_i \cap R_j\}$ | Set of train pairs sharing section $s$ |
| $S^{stop}_i \subseteq R_i$ | Sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop |
| $S^{mon} \subseteq S$ | Monitored sections where delay is penalised |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ through section $s$ under profile $p$ (including occupation time) |
| $v^{in}_{i,p,s},\; v^{out}_{i,p,s}$ | Entry and exit speeds of train $i$ at section $s$ under profile $p$ *(used offline to compute separation constants)* |
| $D^{brake}_{i,p,s}$ | Braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ at section $s$ *(used offline)* |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Leader's separation contribution: clearing/occupation time of train $i$ under profile $p$ at section $s$ |
| $g_{j,q,s}$ | Follower's separation contribution: brake indication time headway of train $j$ under profile $q$ at section $s$, derived from $D^{brake}_{j,q,s}$ and $v^{in}_{j,q,s}$ |
| $\text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} = h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$ | Minimum entry-to-entry time between leader $i$ (profile $p$) and follower $j$ (profile $q$) on shared section $s$ *(precomputed offline from ETCS braking curves — keeps model linear)* |
| $\tau_s$ | Switch release/locking (route setting) time for $s \in S^{SW}$ |
| $a_{i,s}$ | Scheduled (planned) entry time of train $i$ into section $s$ |
| $d_{i,s}$ | Minimum dwell (additional occupation) time of train $i$ at stop section $s \in S^{stop}_i$ |
| $\rho_i$ | Release time: earliest entry of train $i$ into its first section $s_{i,1}$ |
| $\Delta^{max}$ | Maximum allowed delay |
| $w_{i,s}$ | Weight of delay for train $i$ at monitored section $s$ |
| $c^{sp}_{i,p}$ | Cost (penalty) of selecting profile $p$ for train $i$ (higher for slower profiles) |
| $M$ | A sufficiently large constant (big-M) |

> **Assumption (A1):** The separation constant decomposes additively as $\text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} = h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$. This is justified under ETCS Level 2 DTG logic: the leader must clear the section (contribution $h$) and the follower needs its own speed-dependent braking distance plus safety margin (contribution $g$). This decomposition avoids bilinear terms $x_{i,p} \cdot x_{j,q}$.

> **Assumption (A2):** Running times $r_{i,p,s}$ include the time a train physically occupies section $s$, so that entry into the next section implies the previous section is cleared.

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| $t_{i,s}$ | Continuous $\geq 0$ | Actual entry time of train $i$ into section $s \in R_i$ |
| $D_{i,s}$ | Continuous $\geq 0$ | Delay of train $i$ at section $s \in S^{mon}$ |
| $x_{i,p}$ | Binary | $= 1$ if train $i$ selects speed profile $p \in P_i$ |
| $y_{i,j,s}$ | Binary | $= 1$ if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on shared section $s$ |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i} w_{i,s} \, D_{i,s}}_{\text{(a) weighted total delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{sp}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}}_{\text{(b) profile selection penalty}}$$

**Explanation:**
- **(a)** Minimises the weighted sum of delays at monitored exit points (or all sections), encouraging on-time performance with train-specific priorities.
- **(b)** Penalises selection of slower-than-nominal profiles, discouraging unnecessary speed reduction when not needed for conflict resolution.

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Exactly one profile per train

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one speed profile from its available set.

---

### 5.2 Running time / route traversal (linking consecutive sections)

$$t_{i,\,R_i(k+1)} \;\geq\; t_{i,\,R_i(k)} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,\,R_i(k)} \; x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; k = 1, \ldots, n_i - 1$$

Train $i$ cannot enter the next section $R_i(k+1)$ before it has entered the current section $R_i(k)$ plus the running time under its chosen profile. Only the selected profile's running time is active (since exactly one $x_{i,p} = 1$).

---

### 5.3 Minimum dwell time at scheduled stops

$$t_{i,\,R_i(k+1)} \;\geq\; t_{i,\,R_i(k)} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,\,R_i(k)} \, x_{i,p} \;+\; d_{i,\,R_i(k)} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; k : R_i(k) \in S^{stop}_i$$

At stop sections, the train must additionally dwell for at least $d_{i,s}$ time units before departing (entering the next section).

> **Assumption (A3):** Dwell is modelled as an additional minimum occupation time at the stop section, absorbed into the section traversal constraint.

---

### 5.4 Initial condition (release time)

$$t_{i,\,s_{i,1}} \;\geq\; \rho_i \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Train $i$ cannot enter its first section before its release time into the network.

---

### 5.5 No early arrival (entry time bounded below by schedule)

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; a_{i,s} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in R_i$$

Trains cannot enter sections before their scheduled time. *(Optional: remove if early running is permitted.)*

---

### 5.6 Disjunctive conflict constraints — general sections ($s \notin S^{SW}$)

For all $s \in S \setminus S^{SW}$, $(i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$:

$$t_{j,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} h_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} \;-\; M \,(1 - y_{i,j,s})$$

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{j,s} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} h_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} g_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} \;-\; M \, y_{i,j,s}$$

**Explanation:**
- If $y_{i,j,s} = 1$ (train $i$ leads), the first constraint is active: $j$ enters $s$ at least $h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$ after $i$ enters $s$. The second constraint is relaxed by big-M.
- If $y_{i,j,s} = 0$ (train $j$ leads), the second constraint is active with roles reversed, and the first is relaxed.
- The separation $\text{sep} = h + g$ is **linear** in $x$ because exactly one profile binary per train is 1 (A1).

---

### 5.7 Switch-release constraints — switch sections ($s \in S^{SW}$)

For all $s \in S^{SW}$, $(i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$:

$$t_{j,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} \left( r_{i,p,s} \right) x_{i,p} \;+\; \tau_s \;-\; M \,(1 - y_{i,j,s})$$

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{j,s} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} \left( r_{j,q,s} \right) x_{j,q} \;+\; \tau_s \;-\; M \, y_{i,j,s}$$

**Explanation:**
- At switch sections, the *stronger* constraint applies: the follower $j$ cannot enter until the leader $i$ has **cleared** the section (running time $r_{i,p,s}$ elapses) **plus** the switch release/locking time $\tau_s$.
- This models route locking: the interlocking must release the switch before a conflicting route can be set.
- These constraints **replace** (or can coexist with, since they dominate) the general headway constraints for $s \in S^{SW}$.

> **Assumption (A4):** The switch release time $\tau_s$ is section-dependent but train-independent. A more refined model could use $\tau_{i,j,s}$.

---

### 5.8 Delay definition

$$D_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;-\; a_{i,s} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$$

$$D_{i,s} \;\geq\; 0$$

Delay is the excess of actual over scheduled entry time; the non-negativity ensures $D_{i,s} = \max(0, t_{i,s} - a_{i,s})$ at optimality (since delays are penalised in the objective).

---

### 5.9 Maximum delay bound

$$D_{i,s} \;\leq\; \Delta^{max} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$$

No train may accumulate delay exceeding the maximum allowed threshold.

---

## 6. Summary of the Complete Model

$$\min \; \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i} w_{i,s} \, D_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{sp}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}$$

**subject to:**

| # | Constraint | Domain |
|---|-----------|--------|
| (1) | $\sum_{p} x_{i,p} = 1$ | $\forall i$ |
| (2) | $t_{i,R_i(k+1)} \geq t_{i,R_i(k)} + \sum_p r_{i,p,R_i(k)} x_{i,p}$ | $\forall i,\, k=1..n_i{-}1,\; R_i(k) \notin S^{stop}_i$ |
| (3) | $t_{i,R_i(k+1)} \geq t_{i,R_i(k)} + \sum_p r_{i,p,R_i(k)} x_{i,p} + d_{i,R_i(k)}$ | $\forall i,\, k : R_i(k) \in S^{stop}_i$ |
| (4) | $t_{i,s_{i,1}} \geq \rho_i$ | $\forall i$ |
| (5) | $t_{i,s} \geq a_{i,s}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in R_i$ |
| (6a) | $t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_p h_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \sum_q g_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} - M(1{-}y_{i,j,s})$ | $\forall s \notin S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (6b) | $t_{i,s} \geq t_{j,s} + \sum_q h_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} + \sum_p g_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} - M\, y_{i,j,s}$ | $\forall s \notin S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (7a) | $t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_p r_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \tau_s - M(1{-}y_{i,j,s})$ | $\forall s \in S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (7b) | $t_{i,s} \geq t_{j,s} + \sum_q r_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} + \tau_s - M\, y_{i,j,s}$ | $\forall s \in S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (8) | $D_{i,s} \geq t_{i,s} - a_{i,s}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$ |
| (9) | $D_{i,s} \leq \Delta^{max}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$ |
| (10) | $t_{i,s} \geq 0,\; D_{i,s} \geq 0$ | $\forall i,\, s$ |
| (11) | $x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\}$ | $\forall i,\, p \in P_i$ |
| (12) | $y_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$ | $\forall s,\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |

---

## 7. Remarks on Linearity and Model Properties

1. **Linearity of separation:** The bilinear product $x_{i,p} \cdot x_{j,q}$ in $\sum_{p,q} \text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} \, x_{i,p} \, x_{j,q}$ is avoided by the additive decomposition $\text{sep} = h + g$ (A1), yielding $\sum_p h_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \sum_q g_{j,q,s} x_{j,q}$, which is linear.

2. **Alternative linearisation (if decomposition is not valid):** Introduce auxiliary binaries $z_{i,j,s,p,q} \in \{0,1\}$ with McCormick-style constraints:
   $$z_{i,j,s,p,q} \leq x_{i,p}, \quad z_{i,j,s,p,q} \leq x_{j,q}, \quad z_{i,j,s,p,q} \geq x_{i,p} + x_{j,q} - 1$$
   and use $\sum_{p,q} \text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} \, z_{i,j,s,p,q}$ in place of the linear headway terms. This increases the number of binary variables substantially.

3. **Consistency of ordering across sections:** For trains sharing multiple consecutive sections, one may add precedence consistency constraints $y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'}$ for sections $s, s'$ on the same corridor segment to prevent overtaking between stations. *(Optional, depending on network topology.)*

4. **Big-M tuning:** $M$ can be set to $a^{max} + \Delta^{max} + r^{max} - a^{min}$ where $a^{max}, a^{min}$ are the latest/earliest scheduled times and $r^{max}$ is the maximum running/separation time, providing a tight bound.

5. **Model class:** This is a **mixed-integer linear program** (MILP) — all constraints and the objective are linear in the decision variables; integrality arises solely from the binary profile-selection variables $x$ and ordering variables $y$.

messages.content:
Below is the complete, self-contained, linear MILP formulation for Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) under ETCS Level 2 with Dynamic Transmission Generation (DTG) / moving-block-like signalling. The model incorporates the revised switch-release logic, precedence consistency, explicit DTG braking-headway semantics, and hierarchical objective weighting.

---

## 1. Model Description

Consider a set of trains $I = \{1,\dots,n\}$ traversing a railway network composed of sections (block sections, switch sections, and station tracks) $S$. Each train $i$ follows a fixed route $R_i = (s_1, s_2, \dots, s_{|R_i|})$ and must choose a speed profile $p \in P_i$ (e.g., high-speed, medium, low-speed) determining its running times and braking characteristics. Under ETCS L2 DTG, signalling is not constrained by fixed block boundaries; instead, a following train $j$ receives a Movement Authority (MA) up to the rear of the preceding train $i$ minus a safety margin. The critical time separation at the entrance of section $s$ therefore depends on the speed-dependent braking distance of $j$ computed from its entry speed. This is captured through the **braking headway** $g_{j,q,s}$, computed offline from the braking curve starting at entry speed $v^{\text{in}}_{j,q,s}$ over the dynamic braking distance $D^{\text{brake}}_{j,q,s}$, converted to a time headway.

**Objective:** Minimise total weighted train delays (primary) while penalising the use of low-speed profiles (secondary, scaled to be lexicographically subordinate).

---

## 2. Sets, Parameters, and Variables

### Sets
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $S$ | Set of infrastructure sections (including switches), indexed by $s$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of available speed profiles for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i \subseteq S$ | Ordered sequence of sections for train $i$ |
| $S_{\text{sw}} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections requiring route release |
| $P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \subseteq S \times S$ | Pairs of sections $(s, s')$ shared by $i$ and $j$ where overtaking is physically impossible between them, requiring precedence consistency |

### Parameters
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ (includes dwell time if $s$ is a scheduled stop) |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Clearing/occupation time headway of $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ for open (non-switch) sections; typically $h_{i,p,s} \approx r_{i,p,s}$ |
| $g_{j,q,s}$ | Braking headway of follower $j$ with profile $q$ at the entrance of section $s$ under ETCS L2 DTG; computed from the braking curve to ensure $j$ can stop before a conflicting MA endpoint |
| $\tau_s$ | Switch release and locking time for section $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$ (time from leader clearing the switch until the route is free for the follower) |
| $d_{i,s}$ | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $w_{i,s}$ | Weight (penalty) for delay of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p}$ | Penalty for selecting profile $p$ for train $i$; satisfies $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll w_{i,s}$ to ensure lexicographic prioritisation of delay minimisation |
| $M$ | Large constant (Big-M) used to activate/deactivate disjunctive constraints |

### Decision Variables
| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| $t_{i,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Actual entry time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $x_{i,p}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ selects speed profile $p$, 0 otherwise |
| $y_{i,j,s}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$, 0 if $j$ precedes $i$ (defined for all unordered pairs $i \neq j$ sharing section $s$) |

---

## 3. Objective Function

$$
\min \quad \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in R_i} w_{i,s} \, (t_{i,s} - d_{i,s})}_{\text{Primary: weighted delay}} \; + \; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}}_{\text{Secondary: profile penalty}}
$$

*   **Lexicographic scaling:** The profile penalties are scaled such that $\max_{i,p} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll \min_{i,s} w_{i,s}$. This ensures that the optimiser always prefers reducing delay over selecting a faster profile, embedding a lexicographic hierarchy within a single weighted sum.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Profile Selection
Each train must select exactly one speed profile:
$$
\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.1}
$$

### 4.2 Temporal Sequencing (Fixed Route)
Train $i$ must traverse its route in order. The entry time to section $s_{k+1}$ is the entry time to $s_k$ plus the running time through $s_k$ under the selected profile:
$$
t_{i, s_{k+1}} = t_{i, s_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s_k} \, x_{i,p} \quad \forall i \in I,\, k = 1, \dots, |R_i|-1 \tag{5.2}
$$

*Note:* If $s_k$ is a scheduled stop, $r_{i,p,s_k}$ includes the dwell time. No waiting between sections is permitted (implicit in the equality); if buffer time is required, it is absorbed into $r$.

### 4.3 Release Times
A train cannot enter its first section before its scheduled release (availability) time:
$$
t_{i, s_1} \geq d_{i, s_1} \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.3}
$$

### 4.4 Disjunctive Precedence Definition
For every pair of trains $i, j$ ($i \neq j$) sharing section $s$, exactly one must be the leader:
$$
y_{i,j,s} + y_{j,i,s} = 1 \quad \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j \tag{5.4}
$$

### 4.5 Minimum Headway on Open Sections (ETCS L2 DTG)
For any section $s \notin S_{\text{sw}}$ shared by trains $i$ and $j$, if $i$ leads ($y_{i,j,s} = 1$), then $j$ cannot enter $s$ until $i$ has cleared it (occupation time $h$) **plus** $j$’s speed-dependent braking headway ($g$) required under DTG:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \setminus S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.5}
$$

Symmetrically, if $j$ leads, the constraint is enforced via $y_{j,i,s}$ (automatically handled by 5.4 and the quantification over all ordered pairs).

### 4.6 Switch Release with Braking Headway
For switch sections $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$, the separation must account for the physical route release time $\tau_s$ in addition to the follower’s braking requirement. If $i$ leads, $j$ cannot enter the switch until $i$ has traversed it ($r_{i,p,s}$), the switch has been released ($\tau_s$), **and** $j$ has sufficient braking headway ($g_{j,q,s}$) to stop if the route is not yet locked:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \tau_s + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \cap S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.6}
$$

*Consistency check:* Since $r_{i,p,s} + \tau_s \geq h_{i,p,s}$ for switch sections (the release time adds to the clearing time), constraint (5.6) is strictly more restrictive than (5.5), reflecting the additional hazard of a movable switch.

### 4.7 Precedence Consistency (No Overtaking)
For trains $i$ and $j$ sharing multiple consecutive sections where physical overtaking is impossible (e.g., single-track corridors), the precedence order must be identical across all such sections. For each pair $(s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j}$:

$$
y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'} \quad \forall i \neq j,\, (s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \tag{5.7}
$$

This can be linearised as two inequalities or implemented as an equality of binaries (accepted by all MILP solvers).

### 4.8 Variable Domains
$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,s} &\geq 0 && \forall i \in I,\, s \in R_i \\
x_{i,p} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i \in I,\, p \in P_i \\
y_{i,j,s} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j
\end{aligned} \tag{5.8}
$$

---

## 5. Remarks on Model Extensions

**Rerouting (Route Choice):** The model assumes fixed routes $R_i$. To incorporate rerouting, one can introduce binary route-choice variables $z_{i,r}$ for a set of candidate routes $r \in \mathcal{R}_i$, making the running times $r_{i,p,s}$ and headway parameters $h_{i,p,s}, g_{j,q,s}$ dependent on the chosen route (profile-route-dependent). This extension increases the number of binaries and is omitted here to maintain compactness and focus on the CDR logic under fixed paths.

**DTG Parameter Computation:** The braking headways $g_{j,q,s}$ are not decision variables but are computed a priori from the ETCS braking curves (e.g., using the standard braking model with deceleration $a_{\text{est}}$ and safety margins) for every combination of train, profile, and section entry speed, ensuring the MILP remains linear.

2. Add an optional constraint for precedence consistency: for trains i, j sharing multiple sections on the same corridor (i.e., where overtaking is physically impossible between consecutive shared sections), enforce y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'} for all such section pairs (s, s'). Define a set P^{cons}_{i,j} ⊆ S × S of section pairs where consistency must hold.

3. Clarify in the model description that for ETCS L2 DTG signalling, the brake indication point of the follower j is captured through g_{j,q,s}, which is computed offline from the braking curve starting at entry speed v^{in}_{j,q,s} over braking distance D^{brake}_{j,q,s}, converted to a time headway. This is the key DTG enhancement versus conventional fixed-block.

4. Add a brief remark that the model can be extended with rerouting by introducing route choice binaries and making R_i profile-dependent, but this is left out to maintain the fixed-route assumption and keep the model compact.

5. In the objective, clarify that the profile penalty c^{sp}_{i,p} should be much smaller than delay weights w_{i,s} to ensure delay minimisation is the primary objective (lexicographic-style via weight scaling).

Please provide the complete revised model with all these changes incorporated.

response.content:
Below is the complete, self-contained, linear MILP formulation for Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) under ETCS Level 2 with Dynamic Transmission Generation (DTG) / moving-block-like signalling. The model incorporates the revised switch-release logic, precedence consistency, explicit DTG braking-headway semantics, and hierarchical objective weighting.

---

## 1. Model Description

Consider a set of trains $I = \{1,\dots,n\}$ traversing a railway network composed of sections (block sections, switch sections, and station tracks) $S$. Each train $i$ follows a fixed route $R_i = (s_1, s_2, \dots, s_{|R_i|})$ and must choose a speed profile $p \in P_i$ (e.g., high-speed, medium, low-speed) determining its running times and braking characteristics. Under ETCS L2 DTG, signalling is not constrained by fixed block boundaries; instead, a following train $j$ receives a Movement Authority (MA) up to the rear of the preceding train $i$ minus a safety margin. The critical time separation at the entrance of section $s$ therefore depends on the speed-dependent braking distance of $j$ computed from its entry speed. This is captured through the **braking headway** $g_{j,q,s}$, computed offline from the braking curve starting at entry speed $v^{\text{in}}_{j,q,s}$ over the dynamic braking distance $D^{\text{brake}}_{j,q,s}$, converted to a time headway.

**Objective:** Minimise total weighted train delays (primary) while penalising the use of low-speed profiles (secondary, scaled to be lexicographically subordinate).

---

## 2. Sets, Parameters, and Variables

### Sets
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $S$ | Set of infrastructure sections (including switches), indexed by $s$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of available speed profiles for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i \subseteq S$ | Ordered sequence of sections for train $i$ |
| $S_{\text{sw}} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections requiring route release |
| $P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \subseteq S \times S$ | Pairs of sections $(s, s')$ shared by $i$ and $j$ where overtaking is physically impossible between them, requiring precedence consistency |

### Parameters
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ (includes dwell time if $s$ is a scheduled stop) |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Clearing/occupation time headway of $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ for open (non-switch) sections; typically $h_{i,p,s} \approx r_{i,p,s}$ |
| $g_{j,q,s}$ | Braking headway of follower $j$ with profile $q$ at the entrance of section $s$ under ETCS L2 DTG; computed from the braking curve to ensure $j$ can stop before a conflicting MA endpoint |
| $\tau_s$ | Switch release and locking time for section $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$ (time from leader clearing the switch until the route is free for the follower) |
| $d_{i,s}$ | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $w_{i,s}$ | Weight (penalty) for delay of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p}$ | Penalty for selecting profile $p$ for train $i$; satisfies $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll w_{i,s}$ to ensure lexicographic prioritisation of delay minimisation |
| $M$ | Large constant (Big-M) used to activate/deactivate disjunctive constraints |

### Decision Variables
| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| $t_{i,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Actual entry time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $x_{i,p}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ selects speed profile $p$, 0 otherwise |
| $y_{i,j,s}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$, 0 if $j$ precedes $i$ (defined for all unordered pairs $i \neq j$ sharing section $s$) |

---

## 3. Objective Function

$$
\min \quad \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in R_i} w_{i,s} \, (t_{i,s} - d_{i,s})}_{\text{Primary: weighted delay}} \; + \; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}}_{\text{Secondary: profile penalty}}
$$

*   **Lexicographic scaling:** The profile penalties are scaled such that $\max_{i,p} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll \min_{i,s} w_{i,s}$. This ensures that the optimiser always prefers reducing delay over selecting a faster profile, embedding a lexicographic hierarchy within a single weighted sum.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Profile Selection
Each train must select exactly one speed profile:
$$
\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.1}
$$

### 4.2 Temporal Sequencing (Fixed Route)
Train $i$ must traverse its route in order. The entry time to section $s_{k+1}$ is the entry time to $s_k$ plus the running time through $s_k$ under the selected profile:
$$
t_{i, s_{k+1}} = t_{i, s_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s_k} \, x_{i,p} \quad \forall i \in I,\, k = 1, \dots, |R_i|-1 \tag{5.2}
$$

*Note:* If $s_k$ is a scheduled stop, $r_{i,p,s_k}$ includes the dwell time. No waiting between sections is permitted (implicit in the equality); if buffer time is required, it is absorbed into $r$.

### 4.3 Release Times
A train cannot enter its first section before its scheduled release (availability) time:
$$
t_{i, s_1} \geq d_{i, s_1} \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.3}
$$

### 4.4 Disjunctive Precedence Definition
For every pair of trains $i, j$ ($i \neq j$) sharing section $s$, exactly one must be the leader:
$$
y_{i,j,s} + y_{j,i,s} = 1 \quad \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j \tag{5.4}
$$

### 4.5 Minimum Headway on Open Sections (ETCS L2 DTG)
For any section $s \notin S_{\text{sw}}$ shared by trains $i$ and $j$, if $i$ leads ($y_{i,j,s} = 1$), then $j$ cannot enter $s$ until $i$ has cleared it (occupation time $h$) **plus** $j$’s speed-dependent braking headway ($g$) required under DTG:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \setminus S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.5}
$$

Symmetrically, if $j$ leads, the constraint is enforced via $y_{j,i,s}$ (automatically handled by 5.4 and the quantification over all ordered pairs).

### 4.6 Switch Release with Braking Headway
For switch sections $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$, the separation must account for the physical route release time $\tau_s$ in addition to the follower’s braking requirement. If $i$ leads, $j$ cannot enter the switch until $i$ has traversed it ($r_{i,p,s}$), the switch has been released ($\tau_s$), **and** $j$ has sufficient braking headway ($g_{j,q,s}$) to stop if the route is not yet locked:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \tau_s + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \cap S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.6}
$$

*Consistency check:* Since $r_{i,p,s} + \tau_s \geq h_{i,p,s}$ for switch sections (the release time adds to the clearing time), constraint (5.6) is strictly more restrictive than (5.5), reflecting the additional hazard of a movable switch.

### 4.7 Precedence Consistency (No Overtaking)
For trains $i$ and $j$ sharing multiple consecutive sections where physical overtaking is impossible (e.g., single-track corridors), the precedence order must be identical across all such sections. For each pair $(s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j}$:

$$
y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'} \quad \forall i \neq j,\, (s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \tag{5.7}
$$

This can be linearised as two inequalities or implemented as an equality of binaries (accepted by all MILP solvers).

### 4.8 Variable Domains
$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,s} &\geq 0 && \forall i \in I,\, s \in R_i \\
x_{i,p} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i \in I,\, p \in P_i \\
y_{i,j,s} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j
\end{aligned} \tag{5.8}
$$

---

## 5. Remarks on Model Extensions

**Rerouting (Route Choice):** The model assumes fixed routes $R_i$. To incorporate rerouting, one can introduce binary route-choice variables $z_{i,r}$ for a set of candidate routes $r \in \mathcal{R}_i$, making the running times $r_{i,p,s}$ and headway parameters $h_{i,p,s}, g_{j,q,s}$ dependent on the chosen route (profile-route-dependent). This extension increases the number of binaries and is omitted here to maintain compactness and focus on the CDR logic under fixed paths.

**DTG Parameter Computation:** The braking headways $g_{j,q,s}$ are not decision variables but are computed a priori from the ETCS braking curves (e.g., using the standard braking model with deceleration $a_{\text{est}}$ and safety margins) for every combination of train, profile, and section entry speed, ensuring the MILP remains linear.

Based on your input, generate a complete, linear model with variables, objective function and constraints.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

messages.content:
# MILP Model for Conflict Detection and Resolution in Railway Traffic Management

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $S$ | Set of block sections (track-side detection sections), indexed by $s$ |
| $S^{SW} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections |
| $S \setminus S^{SW}$ | Open-line and platform sections |
| $P_i$ | Set of speed profile options for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i = (s_{i,1}, s_{i,2}, \ldots, s_{i,n_i})$ | Ordered route (sequence of sections) for train $i$ |
| $R_i(k)$ | The $k$-th section on train $i$'s route |
| $\mathcal{C}_s = \{(i,j) : i, j \in I, \, i \neq j, \, s \in R_i \cap R_j\}$ | Set of train pairs sharing section $s$ |
| $S^{stop}_i \subseteq R_i$ | Sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop |
| $S^{mon} \subseteq S$ | Monitored sections where delay is penalised |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ through section $s$ under profile $p$ (including occupation time) |
| $v^{in}_{i,p,s},\; v^{out}_{i,p,s}$ | Entry and exit speeds of train $i$ at section $s$ under profile $p$ *(used offline to compute separation constants)* |
| $D^{brake}_{i,p,s}$ | Braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ at section $s$ *(used offline)* |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Leader's separation contribution: clearing/occupation time of train $i$ under profile $p$ at section $s$ |
| $g_{j,q,s}$ | Follower's separation contribution: brake indication time headway of train $j$ under profile $q$ at section $s$, derived from $D^{brake}_{j,q,s}$ and $v^{in}_{j,q,s}$ |
| $\text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} = h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$ | Minimum entry-to-entry time between leader $i$ (profile $p$) and follower $j$ (profile $q$) on shared section $s$ *(precomputed offline from ETCS braking curves — keeps model linear)* |
| $\tau_s$ | Switch release/locking (route setting) time for $s \in S^{SW}$ |
| $a_{i,s}$ | Scheduled (planned) entry time of train $i$ into section $s$ |
| $d_{i,s}$ | Minimum dwell (additional occupation) time of train $i$ at stop section $s \in S^{stop}_i$ |
| $\rho_i$ | Release time: earliest entry of train $i$ into its first section $s_{i,1}$ |
| $\Delta^{max}$ | Maximum allowed delay |
| $w_{i,s}$ | Weight of delay for train $i$ at monitored section $s$ |
| $c^{sp}_{i,p}$ | Cost (penalty) of selecting profile $p$ for train $i$ (higher for slower profiles) |
| $M$ | A sufficiently large constant (big-M) |

> **Assumption (A1):** The separation constant decomposes additively as $\text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} = h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$. This is justified under ETCS Level 2 DTG logic: the leader must clear the section (contribution $h$) and the follower needs its own speed-dependent braking distance plus safety margin (contribution $g$). This decomposition avoids bilinear terms $x_{i,p} \cdot x_{j,q}$.

> **Assumption (A2):** Running times $r_{i,p,s}$ include the time a train physically occupies section $s$, so that entry into the next section implies the previous section is cleared.

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Definition |
|----------|------|------------|
| $t_{i,s}$ | Continuous $\geq 0$ | Actual entry time of train $i$ into section $s \in R_i$ |
| $D_{i,s}$ | Continuous $\geq 0$ | Delay of train $i$ at section $s \in S^{mon}$ |
| $x_{i,p}$ | Binary | $= 1$ if train $i$ selects speed profile $p \in P_i$ |
| $y_{i,j,s}$ | Binary | $= 1$ if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on shared section $s$ |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$\min \; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i} w_{i,s} \, D_{i,s}}_{\text{(a) weighted total delay}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{sp}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}}_{\text{(b) profile selection penalty}}$$

**Explanation:**
- **(a)** Minimises the weighted sum of delays at monitored exit points (or all sections), encouraging on-time performance with train-specific priorities.
- **(b)** Penalises selection of slower-than-nominal profiles, discouraging unnecessary speed reduction when not needed for conflict resolution.

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Exactly one profile per train

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one speed profile from its available set.

---

### 5.2 Running time / route traversal (linking consecutive sections)

$$t_{i,\,R_i(k+1)} \;\geq\; t_{i,\,R_i(k)} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,\,R_i(k)} \; x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; k = 1, \ldots, n_i - 1$$

Train $i$ cannot enter the next section $R_i(k+1)$ before it has entered the current section $R_i(k)$ plus the running time under its chosen profile. Only the selected profile's running time is active (since exactly one $x_{i,p} = 1$).

---

### 5.3 Minimum dwell time at scheduled stops

$$t_{i,\,R_i(k+1)} \;\geq\; t_{i,\,R_i(k)} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,\,R_i(k)} \, x_{i,p} \;+\; d_{i,\,R_i(k)} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; k : R_i(k) \in S^{stop}_i$$

At stop sections, the train must additionally dwell for at least $d_{i,s}$ time units before departing (entering the next section).

> **Assumption (A3):** Dwell is modelled as an additional minimum occupation time at the stop section, absorbed into the section traversal constraint.

---

### 5.4 Initial condition (release time)

$$t_{i,\,s_{i,1}} \;\geq\; \rho_i \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Train $i$ cannot enter its first section before its release time into the network.

---

### 5.5 No early arrival (entry time bounded below by schedule)

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; a_{i,s} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in R_i$$

Trains cannot enter sections before their scheduled time. *(Optional: remove if early running is permitted.)*

---

### 5.6 Disjunctive conflict constraints — general sections ($s \notin S^{SW}$)

For all $s \in S \setminus S^{SW}$, $(i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$:

$$t_{j,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} h_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} \;-\; M \,(1 - y_{i,j,s})$$

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{j,s} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} h_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} g_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} \;-\; M \, y_{i,j,s}$$

**Explanation:**
- If $y_{i,j,s} = 1$ (train $i$ leads), the first constraint is active: $j$ enters $s$ at least $h_{i,p,s} + g_{j,q,s}$ after $i$ enters $s$. The second constraint is relaxed by big-M.
- If $y_{i,j,s} = 0$ (train $j$ leads), the second constraint is active with roles reversed, and the first is relaxed.
- The separation $\text{sep} = h + g$ is **linear** in $x$ because exactly one profile binary per train is 1 (A1).

---

### 5.7 Switch-release constraints — switch sections ($s \in S^{SW}$)

For all $s \in S^{SW}$, $(i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$:

$$t_{j,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{p \in P_i} \left( r_{i,p,s} \right) x_{i,p} \;+\; \tau_s \;-\; M \,(1 - y_{i,j,s})$$

$$t_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{j,s} \;+\; \sum_{q \in P_j} \left( r_{j,q,s} \right) x_{j,q} \;+\; \tau_s \;-\; M \, y_{i,j,s}$$

**Explanation:**
- At switch sections, the *stronger* constraint applies: the follower $j$ cannot enter until the leader $i$ has **cleared** the section (running time $r_{i,p,s}$ elapses) **plus** the switch release/locking time $\tau_s$.
- This models route locking: the interlocking must release the switch before a conflicting route can be set.
- These constraints **replace** (or can coexist with, since they dominate) the general headway constraints for $s \in S^{SW}$.

> **Assumption (A4):** The switch release time $\tau_s$ is section-dependent but train-independent. A more refined model could use $\tau_{i,j,s}$.

---

### 5.8 Delay definition

$$D_{i,s} \;\geq\; t_{i,s} \;-\; a_{i,s} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$$

$$D_{i,s} \;\geq\; 0$$

Delay is the excess of actual over scheduled entry time; the non-negativity ensures $D_{i,s} = \max(0, t_{i,s} - a_{i,s})$ at optimality (since delays are penalised in the objective).

---

### 5.9 Maximum delay bound

$$D_{i,s} \;\leq\; \Delta^{max} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$$

No train may accumulate delay exceeding the maximum allowed threshold.

---

## 6. Summary of the Complete Model

$$\min \; \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i} w_{i,s} \, D_{i,s} \;+\; \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{sp}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}$$

**subject to:**

| # | Constraint | Domain |
|---|-----------|--------|
| (1) | $\sum_{p} x_{i,p} = 1$ | $\forall i$ |
| (2) | $t_{i,R_i(k+1)} \geq t_{i,R_i(k)} + \sum_p r_{i,p,R_i(k)} x_{i,p}$ | $\forall i,\, k=1..n_i{-}1,\; R_i(k) \notin S^{stop}_i$ |
| (3) | $t_{i,R_i(k+1)} \geq t_{i,R_i(k)} + \sum_p r_{i,p,R_i(k)} x_{i,p} + d_{i,R_i(k)}$ | $\forall i,\, k : R_i(k) \in S^{stop}_i$ |
| (4) | $t_{i,s_{i,1}} \geq \rho_i$ | $\forall i$ |
| (5) | $t_{i,s} \geq a_{i,s}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in R_i$ |
| (6a) | $t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_p h_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \sum_q g_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} - M(1{-}y_{i,j,s})$ | $\forall s \notin S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (6b) | $t_{i,s} \geq t_{j,s} + \sum_q h_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} + \sum_p g_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} - M\, y_{i,j,s}$ | $\forall s \notin S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (7a) | $t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_p r_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \tau_s - M(1{-}y_{i,j,s})$ | $\forall s \in S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (7b) | $t_{i,s} \geq t_{j,s} + \sum_q r_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} + \tau_s - M\, y_{i,j,s}$ | $\forall s \in S^{SW},\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |
| (8) | $D_{i,s} \geq t_{i,s} - a_{i,s}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$ |
| (9) | $D_{i,s} \leq \Delta^{max}$ | $\forall i,\, s \in S^{mon} \cap R_i$ |
| (10) | $t_{i,s} \geq 0,\; D_{i,s} \geq 0$ | $\forall i,\, s$ |
| (11) | $x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\}$ | $\forall i,\, p \in P_i$ |
| (12) | $y_{i,j,s} \in \{0,1\}$ | $\forall s,\, (i,j) \in \mathcal{C}_s$ |

---

## 7. Remarks on Linearity and Model Properties

1. **Linearity of separation:** The bilinear product $x_{i,p} \cdot x_{j,q}$ in $\sum_{p,q} \text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} \, x_{i,p} \, x_{j,q}$ is avoided by the additive decomposition $\text{sep} = h + g$ (A1), yielding $\sum_p h_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + \sum_q g_{j,q,s} x_{j,q}$, which is linear.

2. **Alternative linearisation (if decomposition is not valid):** Introduce auxiliary binaries $z_{i,j,s,p,q} \in \{0,1\}$ with McCormick-style constraints:
   $$z_{i,j,s,p,q} \leq x_{i,p}, \quad z_{i,j,s,p,q} \leq x_{j,q}, \quad z_{i,j,s,p,q} \geq x_{i,p} + x_{j,q} - 1$$
   and use $\sum_{p,q} \text{sep}_{i,p,j,q,s} \, z_{i,j,s,p,q}$ in place of the linear headway terms. This increases the number of binary variables substantially.

3. **Consistency of ordering across sections:** For trains sharing multiple consecutive sections, one may add precedence consistency constraints $y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'}$ for sections $s, s'$ on the same corridor segment to prevent overtaking between stations. *(Optional, depending on network topology.)*

4. **Big-M tuning:** $M$ can be set to $a^{max} + \Delta^{max} + r^{max} - a^{min}$ where $a^{max}, a^{min}$ are the latest/earliest scheduled times and $r^{max}$ is the maximum running/separation time, providing a tight bound.

5. **Model class:** This is a **mixed-integer linear program** (MILP) — all constraints and the objective are linear in the decision variables; integrality arises solely from the binary profile-selection variables $x$ and ordering variables $y$.

{"description":"Please revise the MILP model for railway Conflict Detection and Resolution under ETCS Level 2 DTG signalling with the following feedback:

1. In constraint 5.7 (switch-release), the separation for switch sections uses the leader's running time r_{i,p,s} as the clearing time. This is inconsistent with the general headway formulation in 5.6 which uses h_{i,p,s} (clearing/occupation) + g_{j,q,s} (follower braking headway). For switch sections, the correct formulation should ALSO incorporate the follower's speed-dependent braking distance: the follower j must not enter the switch section s before the leader i has cleared it (running time) PLUS the switch release time τ_s, BUT additionally the follower needs its braking headway g_{j,q,s} to be able to stop before the occupied switch if the route is not yet released. So the switch constraint should be: t_{j,s} ≥ t_{i,s} + Σ_p r_{i,p,s} x_{i,p} + τ_s + Σ_q g_{j,q,s} x_{j,q} − M(1−y_{i,j,s}). This makes switch sections strictly more restrictive than open sections (since r + τ + g ≥ h + g when r ≥ h − τ).

2. Add an optional constraint for precedence consistency: for trains i, j sharing multiple sections on the same corridor (i.e., where overtaking is physically impossible between consecutive shared sections), enforce y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'} for all such section pairs (s, s'). Define a set P^{cons}_{i,j} ⊆ S × S of section pairs where consistency must hold.

3. Clarify in the model description that for ETCS L2 DTG signalling, the brake indication point of the follower j is captured through g_{j,q,s}, which is computed offline from the braking curve starting at entry speed v^{in}_{j,q,s} over braking distance D^{brake}_{j,q,s}, converted to a time headway. 4. Add a brief remark that the model can be extended with rerouting by introducing route choice binaries and making R_i profile-dependent, but this is left out to maintain the fixed-route assumption and keep the model compact.

5. In the objective, clarify that the profile penalty c^{sp}_{i,p} should be much smaller than delay weights w_{i,s} to ensure delay minimisation is the primary objective (lexicographic-style via weight scaling).

Please provide the complete revised model with all these changes incorporated."}

messages.content:
Below is the complete, self-contained, linear MILP formulation for Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) under ETCS Level 2 with Dynamic Transmission Generation (DTG) / moving-block-like signalling. The model incorporates the revised switch-release logic, precedence consistency, explicit DTG braking-headway semantics, and hierarchical objective weighting.

---

## 1. Model Description

Consider a set of trains $I = \{1,\dots,n\}$ traversing a railway network composed of sections (block sections, switch sections, and station tracks) $S$. Each train $i$ follows a fixed route $R_i = (s_1, s_2, \dots, s_{|R_i|})$ and must choose a speed profile $p \in P_i$ (e.g., high-speed, medium, low-speed) determining its running times and braking characteristics. Under ETCS L2 DTG, signalling is not constrained by fixed block boundaries; instead, a following train $j$ receives a Movement Authority (MA) up to the rear of the preceding train $i$ minus a safety margin. The critical time separation at the entrance of section $s$ therefore depends on the speed-dependent braking distance of $j$ computed from its entry speed. This is captured through the **braking headway** $g_{j,q,s}$, computed offline from the braking curve starting at entry speed $v^{\text{in}}_{j,q,s}$ over the dynamic braking distance $D^{\text{brake}}_{j,q,s}$, converted to a time headway.

**Objective:** Minimise total weighted train delays (primary) while penalising the use of low-speed profiles (secondary, scaled to be lexicographically subordinate).

---

## 2. Sets, Parameters, and Variables

### Sets
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $S$ | Set of infrastructure sections (including switches), indexed by $s$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of available speed profiles for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i \subseteq S$ | Ordered sequence of sections for train $i$ |
| $S_{\text{sw}} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections requiring route release |
| $P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \subseteq S \times S$ | Pairs of sections $(s, s')$ shared by $i$ and $j$ where overtaking is physically impossible between them, requiring precedence consistency |

### Parameters
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ (includes dwell time if $s$ is a scheduled stop) |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Clearing/occupation time headway of $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ for open (non-switch) sections; typically $h_{i,p,s} \approx r_{i,p,s}$ |
| $g_{j,q,s}$ | Braking headway of follower $j$ with profile $q$ at the entrance of section $s$ under ETCS L2 DTG; computed from the braking curve to ensure $j$ can stop before a conflicting MA endpoint |
| $\tau_s$ | Switch release and locking time for section $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$ (time from leader clearing the switch until the route is free for the follower) |
| $d_{i,s}$ | Scheduled (planned) arrival time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $w_{i,s}$ | Weight (penalty) for delay of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p}$ | Penalty for selecting profile $p$ for train $i$; satisfies $c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll w_{i,s}$ to ensure lexicographic prioritisation of delay minimisation |
| $M$ | Large constant (Big-M) used to activate/deactivate disjunctive constraints |

### Decision Variables
| Symbol | Type | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| $t_{i,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Actual entry time of train $i$ at section $s$ |
| $x_{i,p}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ selects speed profile $p$, 0 otherwise |
| $y_{i,j,s}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | Binary: 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $s$, 0 if $j$ precedes $i$ (defined for all unordered pairs $i \neq j$ sharing section $s$) |

---

## 3. Objective Function

$$
\min \quad \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{s \in R_i} w_{i,s} \, (t_{i,s} - d_{i,s})}_{\text{Primary: weighted delay}} \; + \; \underbrace{\sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \, x_{i,p}}_{\text{Secondary: profile penalty}}
$$

*   **Lexicographic scaling:** The profile penalties are scaled such that $\max_{i,p} c^{\text{sp}}_{i,p} \ll \min_{i,s} w_{i,s}$. This ensures that the optimiser always prefers reducing delay over selecting a faster profile, embedding a lexicographic hierarchy within a single weighted sum.

---

## 4. Constraints

### 4.1 Profile Selection
Each train must select exactly one speed profile:
$$
\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.1}
$$

### 4.2 Temporal Sequencing (Fixed Route)
Train $i$ must traverse its route in order. The entry time to section $s_{k+1}$ is the entry time to $s_k$ plus the running time through $s_k$ under the selected profile:
$$
t_{i, s_{k+1}} = t_{i, s_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s_k} \, x_{i,p} \quad \forall i \in I,\, k = 1, \dots, |R_i|-1 \tag{5.2}
$$

*Note:* If $s_k$ is a scheduled stop, $r_{i,p,s_k}$ includes the dwell time. No waiting between sections is permitted (implicit in the equality); if buffer time is required, it is absorbed into $r$.

### 4.3 Release Times
A train cannot enter its first section before its scheduled release (availability) time:
$$
t_{i, s_1} \geq d_{i, s_1} \quad \forall i \in I \tag{5.3}
$$

### 4.4 Disjunctive Precedence Definition
For every pair of trains $i, j$ ($i \neq j$) sharing section $s$, exactly one must be the leader:
$$
y_{i,j,s} + y_{j,i,s} = 1 \quad \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j \tag{5.4}
$$

### 4.5 Minimum Headway on Open Sections (ETCS L2 DTG)
For any section $s \notin S_{\text{sw}}$ shared by trains $i$ and $j$, if $i$ leads ($y_{i,j,s} = 1$), then $j$ cannot enter $s$ until $i$ has cleared it (occupation time $h$) **plus** $j$’s speed-dependent braking headway ($g$) required under DTG:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \setminus S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.5}
$$

Symmetrically, if $j$ leads, the constraint is enforced via $y_{j,i,s}$ (automatically handled by 5.4 and the quantification over all ordered pairs).

### 4.6 Switch Release with Braking Headway
For switch sections $s \in S_{\text{sw}}$, the separation must account for the physical route release time $\tau_s$ in addition to the follower’s braking requirement. If $i$ leads, $j$ cannot enter the switch until $i$ has traversed it ($r_{i,p,s}$), the switch has been released ($\tau_s$), **and** $j$ has sufficient braking headway ($g_{j,q,s}$) to stop if the route is not yet locked:

$$
t_{j,s} \geq t_{i,s} + \sum_{p \in P_i} r_{i,p,s} \, x_{i,p} + \tau_s + \sum_{q \in P_j} g_{j,q,s} \, x_{j,q} - M (1 - y_{i,j,s}) \quad \forall i \neq j,\, s \in (R_i \cap R_j) \cap S_{\text{sw}} \tag{5.6}
$$

*Consistency check:* Since $r_{i,p,s} + \tau_s \geq h_{i,p,s}$ for switch sections (the release time adds to the clearing time), constraint (5.6) is strictly more restrictive than (5.5), reflecting the additional hazard of a movable switch.

### 4.7 Precedence Consistency (No Overtaking)
For trains $i$ and $j$ sharing multiple consecutive sections where physical overtaking is impossible (e.g., single-track corridors), the precedence order must be identical across all such sections. For each pair $(s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j}$:

$$
y_{i,j,s} = y_{i,j,s'} \quad \forall i \neq j,\, (s, s') \in P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \tag{5.7}
$$

This can be linearised as two inequalities or implemented as an equality of binaries (accepted by all MILP solvers).

### 4.8 Variable Domains
$$
\begin{aligned}
t_{i,s} &\geq 0 && \forall i \in I,\, s \in R_i \\
x_{i,p} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i \in I,\, p \in P_i \\
y_{i,j,s} &\in \{0,1\} && \forall i, j \in I,\, i \neq j,\, s \in R_i \cap R_j
\end{aligned} \tag{5.8}
$$

---

## 5. Remarks on Model Extensions

**Rerouting (Route Choice):** The model assumes fixed routes $R_i$. To incorporate rerouting, one can introduce binary route-choice variables $z_{i,r}$ for a set of candidate routes $r \in \mathcal{R}_i$, making the running times $r_{i,p,s}$ and headway parameters $h_{i,p,s}, g_{j,q,s}$ dependent on the chosen route (profile-route-dependent). This extension increases the number of binaries and is omitted here to maintain compactness and focus on the CDR logic under fixed paths.

**DTG Parameter Computation:** The braking headways $g_{j,q,s}$ are not decision variables but are computed a priori from the ETCS braking curves (e.g., using the standard braking model with deceleration $a_{\text{est}}$ and safety margins) for every combination of train, profile, and section entry speed, ensuring the MILP remains linear.

The critical time separation at the entrance of section $s$ therefore depends on the speed-dependent braking distance of $j$ computed from its entry speed. **Objective:** Minimise total weighted train delays (primary) while penalising the use of low-speed profiles (secondary, scaled to be lexicographically subordinate).

---

| $S$ | Set of infrastructure sections (including switches), indexed by $s$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of available speed profiles for train $i$, indexed by $p, q$ |
| $R_i \subseteq S$ | Ordered sequence of sections for train $i$ |
| $S_{\text{sw}} \subseteq S$ | Subset of switch sections requiring route release |
| $P^{\text{cons}}_{i,j} \subseteq S \times S$ | Pairs of sections $(s, s')$ shared by $i$ and $j$ where overtaking is physically impossible between them, requiring precedence consistency |

### Parameters
| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $r_{i,p,s}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ (includes dwell time if $s$ is a scheduled stop) |
| $h_{i,p,s}$ | Clearing/occupation time headway of $i$ on section $s$ under profile $p$ for open (non-switch) sections; typically $h_{i,p,s} \approx r_{i,p,s}$ |

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

Below is a complete Python implementation using **PuLP** (open-source, works with CBC solver by default). The code includes full linearization of the bilinear terms $x_{i,s_i} \cdot x_{j,s_j}$ that arise in the speed-dependent separation constraints.
