Objective: minimize total weighted positive deviation from scheduled arrival times (total delay) plus small penalty on profile changes. Constraints: each train picks one profile; timing propagation along route t^out = t^in + running time (dependent on selected profile via big-M linearization); dwell time minima at stops; section capacity: for each pair (i,j) sharing section b, disjunctive (big-M) constraints with speed-dependent separation: t^{in}_{j,b} >= t^{out}_{i,b} + h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} - M(1-y_{i,j,b}) and symmetric, where h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} derives from braking distance d_{i,p} (brake indication point can lie anywhere, end of authority at section end); switch sections impose additional locking time; release times for delayed events; optional rerouting binaries z_{i,r} choosing one route among alternatives. Model must be linear (MILP), complete with all equations, and note assumptions (e.g., linear approximation of braking distance to speed classes via profiles).

response.content:
# Conflict Detection and Resolution MILP for Railway Traffic Management under ETCS Level 2 DTG Signalling

## 1. Complete Model Formulation

### 1.1 Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, $i \in I$ |
| $B$ | Set of all track sections (blocks), $b \in B$ |
| $B^{SW} \subset B$ | Subset of **switch sections** (require additional locking time) |
| $B^{PL} = B \setminus B^{SW}$ | Subset of plain track sections |
| $B^{stop}_i \subseteq R_i$ | Sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop |
| $R_i$ | Set of alternative routes for train $i$, $r \in R_i$ |
| $R_i(r) = (b_{i,r,1}, b_{i,r,2}, \ldots, b_{i,r,n_{i,r}})$ | Ordered sequence of sections for route $r$ of train $i$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of speed profile options for train $i$, $p \in P_i$ |
| $S$ | Set of discrete event time indices (for possible discretization of releases) |

For the remainder, when a single route is considered (or after route selection), we denote by $(b_{i,1}, b_{i,2}, \ldots, b_{i,n_i})$ the sequence of sections along the selected route of train $i$. We write $b \prec_i b'$ when $b$ immediately precedes $b'$ in the route of train $i$.

### 1.2 Parameters

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $\tau^{A}_{i}$ | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at its final destination |
| $\tau^{A}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at section $b$ (if applicable) |
| $\tau^{D}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled departure time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $\delta^{min}_{i,b}$ | Minimum dwell time of train $i$ at stop section $b \in B^{stop}_i$ |
| $rt_{i,b,p}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $b$ under speed profile $p$ |
| $bt_{i,b,p}$ | Blocking (occupation) time of section $b$ by train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $d_{i,p}$ | Braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ (speed-dependent) |
| $d^{sight}_{i,p}$ | Sighting/reaction distance for train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $d^{sight+brake}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$ | Total DTG approach distance |
| $t^{clear}_{i}$ | Clearing time (time for full train to vacate a section after entry) |
| $t^{route}_{b}$ | Interlocking/route-setting time for section $b$ |
| $t^{lock}_{b}$ | Additional locking time for switch section $b \in B^{SW}$ |
| $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ | DTG separation headway: minimum time interval that train $i$ under profile $p$ must allow before another train can enter section $b$ (see §2.3) |
| $t^{rel}_{i,b}$ | Release time (earliest possible entry) of train $i$ at section $b$ |
| $w_i$ | Weight (priority) of train $i$ in the objective |
| $\lambda$ | Small penalty coefficient for profile changes (profile deviating from nominal) |
| $p^{nom}_i$ | Nominal (default) speed profile for train $i$ |
| $M$ | Big-M constant (sufficiently large positive number) |
| $T^{max}$ | Time horizon upper bound |
| $T^{min}$ | Time horizon lower bound |

### 1.3 Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Domain | Definition |
|----------|------|--------|------------|
| $x_{i,p}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ uses speed profile $p$ |
| $z_{i,r}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ uses route $r \in R_i$ |
| $t^{in}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $[T^{min}, T^{max}]$ | Entry time of train $i$ into section $b$ |
| $t^{out}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $[T^{min}, T^{max}]$ | Exit time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $y_{i,j,b}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on shared section $b$ |
| $d_i$ | Continuous | $\geq 0$ | Positive deviation (delay) of train $i$ at final destination |
| $u_i$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ deviates from nominal profile (used for penalty) |

---

### 1.4 Objective Function

$$\min \; \sum_{i \in I} w_i \cdot d_i \; + \; \lambda \sum_{i \in I} u_i$$

**Interpretation:** Minimize total weighted positive deviation from scheduled arrival times at final destinations, plus a small penalty for speed profile changes relative to nominal profiles (encouraging solution stability).

---

### 1.5 Constraints

#### (C1) Exactly One Speed Profile per Train

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one speed profile.

---

#### (C2) Exactly One Route per Train

$$\sum_{r \in R_i} z_{i,r} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one route from its set of alternatives.

---

#### (C3) Profile Deviation Indicator

$$u_i \geq 1 - x_{i,p^{nom}_i} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

If the nominal profile is not selected ($x_{i,p^{nom}_i} = 0$), then $u_i = 1$ and the penalty is incurred. Since we minimize, $u_i$ will be pushed to $0$ when possible.

---

#### (C4) Timing Propagation Along Route — Running Time (Big-M Linearization over Profiles)

For each train $i \in I$ and each pair of consecutive sections $(b_k, b_{k+1})$ along its route sequence:

$$t^{out}_{i,b_k} \geq t^{in}_{i,b_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b_k,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; \forall \, b_k \in \text{route of } i$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} = t^{out}_{i,b_k} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; b_{k+1} \text{ follows } b_k \text{ in route of } i$$

**Note:** The running time constraint uses the linear expression $\sum_p rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p}$ which selects the correct running time via the profile binary. This is already linear (no additional big-M needed) because $x_{i,p}$ multiplies a constant parameter $rt_{i,b,p}$, producing a bilinear term that is linear since $x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\}$.

More precisely, the constraint is:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; \forall \, b \text{ on route of } i$$

When route selection binaries $z_{i,r}$ are active, we additionally enforce that times are only constrained for sections on the selected route:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall \, i, r \in R_i, b \in R_i(r)$$

---

#### (C5) Minimum Dwell Time at Scheduled Stops

$$t^{out}_{i,b} - t^{in}_{i,b} \geq \delta^{min}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; b \in B^{stop}_i$$

At stop sections, the total occupancy (entry to exit) must be at least the running time plus the minimum dwell time.

---

#### (C6) Release Times (Earliest Entry)

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{i,1}} \geq t^{rel}_{i,b_{i,1}} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

The first section entry for each train cannot precede its release time (which may account for upstream delays or scheduled departure).

---

#### (C7) Section Capacity / Conflict Resolution — DTG Separation

For each pair of trains $(i, j)$, $i \neq j$, sharing a section $b \in B$:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - y_{i,j,b})$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + \sum_{p \in P_j} h^{DTG}_{j,b,p} \cdot x_{j,p} - M \cdot y_{i,j,b}$$

$$\forall \, (i,j) \in I \times I, \; i \neq j, \; \forall \, b \in B: b \in R_i \cap R_j$$

**Semantics of $y_{i,j,b}$:** When $y_{i,j,b} = 1$, train $i$ goes first on section $b$ and the first constraint becomes active (forcing $j$ to wait until $i$ clears plus the DTG headway). When $y_{i,j,b} = 0$, the second constraint becomes active (forcing $i$ to wait for $j$).

---

#### (C8) DTG Headway Definition (Speed-Dependent Separation)

The DTG headway parameter $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ is computed offline as:

$$h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} = \frac{d^{sight+brake}_{i,p}}{v_{i,p,b}} + t^{clear}_i + t^{route}_b$$

where:
- $v_{i,p,b}$ is the speed of train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$ (parameter),
- $d^{sight+brake}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$ is the total distance the driver/system needs from the brake indication point to the End of Authority (EoA),
- $t^{clear}_i$ is the clearing time for the train to fully exit,
- $t^{route}_b$ is the interlocking route-setting time.

**Key DTG modelling assumption:** Under ETCS Level 2 DTG, the brake indication point can lie anywhere along the track (not just at block boundaries). The End of Authority is the section end. Thus, the minimum separation time for a following train is determined by the time for the leading train to travel the sighting + braking distance at its current speed, plus clearing and route-setting margins.

---

#### (C9) Switch Section Additional Locking

For switch sections $b \in B^{SW}$, the separation constraints are augmented:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} + t^{lock}_b - M \cdot (1 - y_{i,j,b})$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + \sum_{p \in P_j} h^{DTG}_{j,b,p} \cdot x_{j,p} + t^{lock}_b - M \cdot y_{i,j,b}$$

$$\forall \, (i,j), \; i \neq j, \; \forall \, b \in B^{SW}: b \in R_i \cap R_j$$

The additional $t^{lock}_b$ accounts for the longer interlocking locking time required when a switch (turnout) is involved.

---

#### (C10) Delay Computation (Positive Deviation from Scheduled Arrival)

$$d_i \geq t^{in}_{i,b^{final}_i} - \tau^{A}_{i} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

$$d_i \geq 0 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

The delay variable $d_i$ captures only the **positive** deviation (tardiness) from the scheduled arrival time at the final section.

---

#### (C11) Route Consistency (Optional Rerouting)

When multiple routes are available, constraints (C4) and (C7)–(C9) are only enforced for sections on the selected route. This is achieved by conditioning with $z_{i,r}$:

For timing propagation on route $r$:
$$t^{out}_{i,b_k} \geq t^{in}_{i,b_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b_k,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall \, i, r \in R_i, \; b_k \in R_i(r)$$

For conflict resolution, only pairs $(i,j)$ whose selected routes share section $b$ need constraints. This can be enforced by:

$$y_{i,j,b} \leq \sum_{r \in R_i: \, b \in R_i(r)} z_{i,r} \quad \forall \, i, j, b$$

$$y_{i,j,b} \leq \sum_{r \in R_j: \, b \in R_j(r)} z_{i,r} \quad \forall \, i, j, b$$

(These ensure $y_{i,j,b}$ is only meaningful when both trains actually traverse $b$.)

Alternatively, the conflict constraints can be relaxed with an additional $-M(2 - z_{i,r} - z_{j,r'})$ term when both routes must include $b$.

---

#### (C12) Binary and Continuous Variable Bounds

$$x_{i,p} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; p \in P_i$$

$$z_{i,r} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; r \in R_i$$

$$y_{i,j,b} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, (i,j), b$$

$$u_i \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

$$T^{min} \leq t^{in}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall \, i, b$$

$$T^{min} \leq t^{out}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall \, i, b$$

$$d_i \geq 0 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

---

## 2. Explanation of Model Elements

### 2.1 Speed Profile Selection (C1, C3)

Each train selects exactly one speed profile from its feasible set $P_i$. A speed profile defines a complete speed trajectory: running times $rt_{i,b,p}$ on each section and associated braking distances $d_{i,p}$. This is the mechanism by which different speed classes (e.g., line speed vs. reduced speed) affect both running time and the DTG separation headway. The penalty variable $u_i$ and coefficient $\lambda$ discourage unnecessary deviations from the nominal profile, promoting solution stability and driver comfort.

### 2.2 Timing Propagation (C4, C5, C6)

Train movement along its route is modelled as a sequence of section entries and exits. The entry into the next section equals the exit from the previous one ($t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} = t^{out}_{i,b_k}$). The exit time from a section is the entry time plus the running time, which depends on the selected speed profile. At scheduled stops, an additional minimum dwell time is imposed. Release times prevent trains from starting before they are physically or operationally ready.

### 2.3 DTG Headway Derivation (C8)

This is the core ETCS Level 2 DTG-specific element. Under DTG signalling:
- There are **no fixed block signals**; the movement authority extends continuously to the end of the authority (section end).
- The brake indication point (BIP) is the location where the train must begin braking to stop before the EoA. It can lie **anywhere** along the track.
- The minimum separation between two trains on the same section is the time needed for the leading train to travel from the BIP to the EoA, plus clearing and interlocking margins.

The separation distance is:
$$d^{sep}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$$

This is the sum of the **sighting/reaction distance** (distance travelled during the driver's/system's reaction time before braking commences) and the **braking distance** (distance to come to a stop or reach the target speed).

The headway time is then:
$$h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} = \frac{d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}}{v_{i,p,b}} + t^{clear}_i + t^{route}_b$$

The division by speed converts the spatial separation to a temporal one. Since different profiles $p$ imply different speeds $v_{i,p,b}$ and different braking distances $d_{i,p}$, the headway is profile-dependent and is activated via the $x_{i,p}$ binaries.

### 2.4 Conflict Resolution (C7, C9)

The pairwise disjunctive (big-M) constraints with binary variables $y_{i,j,b}$ resolve conflicts on shared sections. For any two trains sharing a section:
- Either train $i$ precedes $j$ (when $y_{i,j,b} = 1$): train $j$ cannot enter until train $i$ has exited plus the DTG headway.
- Or train $j$ precedes $i$ (when $y_{i,j,b} = 0$): symmetric constraint.

For **switch sections**, the additional locking time $t^{lock}_b$ is added to both constraints. This reflects the operational reality that switches require longer interlocking locking before the route can be set for the next train (due to mechanical locking, flank protection, and overlap release).

### 2.5 Objective Function

The objective minimizes:
1. **Total weighted delay**: $\sum_i w_i \cdot d_i$ where $d_i$ is the positive deviation from the scheduled arrival time at the train's destination. Higher-priority trains (e.g., high-speed passenger services) receive larger weights $w_i$.
2. **Profile change penalty**: $\lambda \sum_i u_i$ where $\lambda$ is small (e.g., $0.01$). This acts as a regularization term, ensuring that speed profile changes are only used when they meaningfully reduce delay.

### 2.6 Optional Rerouting (C2, C11)

When alternative routes exist, binary variables $z_{i,r}$ select one route per train. All timing and conflict constraints are conditioned on route selection via big-M terms. This allows the model to reroute trains around conflicts when beneficial, subject to the constraint that all timing and capacity constraints are only enforced on the actually selected route.

---

## 3. Assumptions and Simplifications

### 3.1 Linearization of Braking Distance

The braking distance $d_{i,p}$ is a nonlinear function of speed (typically $d \propto v^2 / (2a)$ for constant deceleration $a$). In this MILP, we assume:

> **Assumption A1:** The continuous braking-distance-to-speed relationship is **discretized into speed classes** represented by the profiles $P_i$. Each profile $p$ corresponds to a specific speed (or speed trajectory) with a pre-computed braking distance $d_{i,p}$. This makes the separation constraints linear.

### 3.2 Deterministic Parameters

All parameters (running times, headways, scheduled times) are assumed deterministic and known. Stochastic variations (e.g., driver behaviour, weather) are not modelled.

### 3.3 Fixed Train Lengths and Clearing Times

Train lengths and clearing times are fixed parameters. The clearing time $t^{clear}_i$ already incorporates the train length divided by its speed under each profile.

### 3.4 Big-M Formulation

The disjunctive constraints use big-M. The value of $M$ must be sufficiently large (e.g., $M = T^{max} + \max_{i,b,p} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$) but as small as possible for computational efficiency.

### 3.5 Single-Direction Sections

Each section $b$ is used in one direction at a time. For bidirectional sections, additional constraints or separate section identifiers per direction are needed.

### 3.6 Infinite Capacity at Platforms

Platform capacity is not explicitly modelled; it is assumed that platform tracks are available when trains arrive. This can be relaxed by treating platform tracks as sections with capacity constraints.

---

## 4. Summary Table of Constraints

| Constraint | Type | Count |
|------------|------|-------|
| (C1) Profile selection | Equality | $|I|$ |
| (C2) Route selection | Equality | $|I|$ |
| (C3) Profile deviation | Inequality | $|I|$ |
| (C4) Running time | Inequality | $\sum_i |R_i|$ |
| (C5) Dwell time | Inequality | $\sum_i |B^{stop}_i|$ |
| (C6) Release time | Inequality | $|I|$ |
| (C7) Conflict (plain) | Disjunctive pair | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B|)$ |
| (C9) Conflict (switch) | Disjunctive pair | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B^{SW}|)$ |
| (C10) Delay computation | Inequality | $2|I|$ |
| (C11) Route consistency | Inequality | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B| \cdot |R|)$ |
| (C12) Bounds | Domain | All variables |

---

## 5. Extension Notes

- **Rolling horizon**: The model can be embedded in a rolling-horizon framework where it is re-solved periodically as new information (delays, disruptions) arrives.
- **Energy-aware profiles**: The speed profiles $P_i$ can be extended to include energy-optimal trajectories, adding an energy term to the objective.
- **Robustness**: Buffer times can be added to headways $h^{DTG}$ to absorb minor perturbations.
- **Passenger connections**: Additional constraints can enforce minimum connection times for passenger transfers at stations.

Introduction

Worldwide, railways are experiencing a continuously increasing travel demand. The existing railway networks have limited capacity and fewer and fewer extension possibilities due to the costly and land-consuming infrastructure. Especially at capacity bottlenecks such as in and around stations, extensions are often not available. To fulfil future railway demand in a different way, advanced signalling systems such as distance-to-go (DTG) systems are developed as capacityincreasing alternatives to conventional fixed-block multi-aspect signalling with automatic train protection systems.

In conventional fixed-block systems, the track is partitioned into blocks of fixed lengths which can be occupied by at most one train at a time.

The block entries are protected by trackside multi-aspect signals which indicate whether an approaching train can proceed, needs to start braking or is required to stop. The automatic train protection system supervises that the trains follow the signal aspects and intervenes when a train does not start braking after a brake indication. Hence, train separation distances are determined based on a number of blocks of fixed length.

Fixed-block DTG systems feature radio-based cab signalling and continuous braking curve supervision from the train front position to the block (or section) entry corresponding to the train’s end of movement authority (MA), i.e., the permission to move to a specific location under supervision. With this, brake indications no longer need to be provided at the entry of a block. Moreover, train separation distances become speed-dependent due to the approach distance to the first occupied block being based on the train’s absolute braking distance.

For effective railway operations, real-time traffic management is crucial. In case of small delays originating from variations in rolling stock, dwell times and driver behaviour, traffic management can apply rescheduling measures such as retiming, reordering and local rerouting to resolve track conflicts while minimising the delay propagation in the network. To support human dispatchers in taking mathematically optimised rescheduling decisions, conflict detection and resolution (CDR) models describing variants of the real-time railway traffic management or rescheduling problem are developed (Cacchiani et al., 2014; Pellegrini et al., 2014). In short, the problem can be formally described as follows: given a railway network and timetable together with delayed events, find a new timetable by rescheduling trains such that all track conflicts are resolved and total delay (or other relevant objective) is minimised.

The existing CDR models mostly refer to conventional fixed-block signalling systems. As a result, they are typically microscopic models that inherently rely on the discretisation of the track into fixed blocks. Moreover, they generally neglect changes in the speed profile to fit the adjusted timetable (Reynolds et al., 2022). Hence, these models cannot accurately capture the speed-dependent separation distances typical for DTG signalling due to the implementation of braking curve supervision (Versluis et al., 2024).

In this paper, we address the research gap regarding CDR for DTG signalling by developing a CDR model for DTG and applying it to assess the operational relevance of modelling CDR for DTG. To obtain a model that represents and identifies optimised rescheduling decisions for DTG railway operations, we propose enhancements for existing CDR models. The enhancements include the introduction of speed profile options and train blocking times considering train- and speed-dependent braking distances. These two enhancements are significant as they are crucial in enabling the modelling of train- and speed-dependent brake indication points in CDR models. As a proof of concept, we incorporate the enhancements into the state-of-the-art CDR model of RECIFE-MILP (Pellegrini et al., 2015), together with a distinction between switches and the rest of the track. The resulting model is assessed through a comparative analysis with the original one for conventional fixed-block signalling in two case studies, specifically in terms of total train delay and rescheduling decisions.

With this, the main contributions of the paper are:

A modelling approach for enhancing conflict detection and resolution models to apply to distance-to-go signalling, introducing train- and speed-dependent train separation and brake indication points.

A mixed-integer linear programming model for conflict detection and resolution under distance-to-go signalling, obtained by integrating distance-to-go principles into the state-of-the-art RECIFE-MILP model.

A comparative analysis illustrating the operational relevance of incorporating distance-to-go principles into conflict detection and resolution modelling, as different rescheduling decisions achieving reductions in total train delay are proposed.

The paper is organised as follows. In Section 2, the state-of-the-art related to the modelling of CDR for DTG signalling is provided.

Section 3 describes the enhancement approach for CDR models to describe DTG signalling.

The mathematical formulation of the fixed-block CDR model RECIFE-MILP enhanced for DTG signalling is presented in Section 4. Section 5 presents the results of the comparative analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper. State-of-the-art in conflict detection and resolution for distance-to-go signalling In this section, we provide an overview of the state-of-the-art relevant for the topic of modelling CDR under DTG signalling. Section 2.1 focuses on DTG signalling as the de-facto standard in the development of next-generation signalling systems. Section 2.2 provides an overview on modelling approaches for CDR existing in the literature.

2.1 Distance-to-go signalling systems In the development of next-generation signalling systems, DTG is the de-facto standard. For the mainline railways, DTG signalling is included within the European Train Control System (ETCS) and the Chinese Train Control System (CTCS). For metro lines, Communication-Based Train Control (CBTC) applies DTG signalling principles. Examples of deployed DTG systems are the fixed-block ETCS Level 2 with Trackside Train Detection (TTD) and the similar CTCS Level 3. The latter is designed for the Chinese high-speed (up to 300 km/h) railway lines (Xu et al., 2017). In this paper, we focus on ETCS Level 2 with TTD, hereafter referred to as ETCS L2, which is implemented on freight and passenger railways throughout the world (European Rail Supply Industry Association, 2022).

To enable cab signalling, ETCS L2 features radio communication between a radio block centre on the trackside and the trains as follows. The radio block centre receives train position information from a train. This information supports the request for a route extension to the interlocking system. Based on safety logic and input from TTD, the interlocking system sets and locks a new route for the train. As a next step, the radio block centre updates the MA before sending it to the train. With the received MA, the train recomputes and supervises a dynamic speed profile including continuous braking curves.

Corresponding to the braking curves, the brake indication point for a train can lie anywhere along the track. The end of authority, however, is consistently set at the end of a block or TTD section (TDS). The TDSs correspond to the parts of the track in which the presence of a train is automatically detected. Whether the end of authority corresponds to a block or TDS depends on the implemented ETCS L2 variant. It can also depend on whether it is on the open line, in a station or around switches. A schematic representation of the ETCS L2 system is provided in Figure 1. In the figure, two trains at the speed-dependent minimum separation distance are included.

Figure 1: Schematic layout of the minimum separation between two trains in a speed-distance diagram under ETCS L2 with (block) section boundaries, radio block centre (RBC) and radio communication (GSM-R). The separation is related to the brake indication point (IP) and the end of authority (EoA) depending on the braking curve.

Within ETCS and CTCS, more advanced application levels are being developed, but not yet deployed.

In particular, ETCS Level 2 with onboard train integrity monitoring (TIM), previously known as ETCS Level 3. This allows the end of authority to be located at the end of the last free virtual (non-physical) block, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Virtual Block, or even at a safety margin behind the rear position of a moving train, e.g., in ETCS Level 2 Moving Block (European Railway Agency, 2016).

Model 1:
Here is a complete, linear Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation for the Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) model under ETCS Level 2 DTG signalling, extending the RECIFE-MILP architecture.

---

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $B$ | Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $b$ |
| $B^{sw} \subseteq B$ | Subset of switch sections (requiring interlocking) |
| $B^{pl} \subseteq B$ | Subset of plain track sections |
| $R_i$ | Set of candidate routes for train $i$, indexed by $r$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of discrete speed profile options for train $i$, indexed by $p$ (each profile defines running times and a braking-distance class) |
| $T$ | Set of discrete event time points (for release/delay modelling) |
| $S_i \subseteq B$ | Subset of sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop (dwell) |
| $B_{i,r} \subseteq B$ | Ordered sequence of sections forming route $r$ of train $i$ |

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Unit | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| $\tau^{arr}_{i,b}$ | s | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at section $b$ (timetable) |
| $\tau^{dep}_{i,b}$ | s | Scheduled departure time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $D^{min}_{i,b}$ | s | Minimum dwell time for train $i$ at stop $b \in S_i$ |
| $\rho_{i,b,p}$ | s | Running time of train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$ |
| $h^{DTG}_{i,p,b}$ | s | Minimum time headway (blocking time) imposed by train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$. Derived from braking distance $d_{i,p}$ via linear approximation: $h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} = \alpha_b \cdot d_{i,p} + \beta_b$, where $\alpha_b, \beta_b$ encode sighting/reaction, clearing, and safety margins for the DTG logic |
| $h^{lock}_{b}$ | s | Additional route-setting/interlocking time for switch section $b \in B^{sw}$ |
| $r^{min}_{i,b}$ | s | Release time (earliest possible entry) for train $i$ at section $b$ (accounts for delayed upstream events) |
| $w_i$ | – | Weight (priority) of train $i$ in the objective |
| $\lambda$ | – | Small penalty weight for profile changes |
| $\hat{p}_i$ | – | Nominal (planned) speed profile for train $i$ |
| $M$ | s | Big-M constant (e.g., scheduling horizon length) |

**Derived Parameters for Route Selection:**
If rerouting is enabled, let $B_{i,r}$ denote the sections of route $r$, and define incidence parameters:
- $\delta_{i,r,b} = 1$ if section $b \in B_{i,r}$, 0 otherwise.

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Domain | Description |
|----------|------|--------|-------------|
| $x_{i,p}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $i$ selects speed profile $p \in P_i$ |
| $z_{i,r}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $i$ selects route $r \in R_i$ (optional; if $|R_i|=1$, fix $z_{i,r}=1$) |
| $t^{in}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Entry time of train $i$ into section $b$ |
| $t^{out}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Exit time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $y_{i,j,b}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on shared section $b$ |
| $d^{+}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Positive deviation (delay) from scheduled arrival at section $b$ |

**Domain constraints:**
$$t^{in}_{i,b}, t^{out}_{i,b} \in [0, T^{max}], \quad y_{i,j,b} \in \{0,1\}, \quad x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\}, \quad z_{i,r} \in \{0,1\}$$

## 4. Objective Function

Minimize total weighted delay plus a small penalty on profile deviations:

$$\min \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{b \in S_i} w_i \cdot d^{+}_{i,b} + \lambda \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{chg}_{i,p} \cdot x_{i,p}$$

where $c^{chg}_{i,p} = 0$ if $p = \hat{p}_i$ (nominal profile), else $c^{chg}_{i,p} = 1$.

The delay variables are defined by:
$$d^{+}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} - \tau^{arr}_{i,b} \quad \forall i \in I, b \in S_i$$
$$d^{+}_{i,b} \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in I, b \in S_i$$

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Profile and Route Selection
Each train selects exactly one speed profile and one route:

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I$$

$$\sum_{r \in R_i} z_{i,r} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I$$

*Linking routes to sections (activation):* A train can only occupy sections belonging to its chosen route. Let $\mathcal{B}_i = \bigcup_{r \in R_i} B_{i,r}$. For $b \notin \mathcal{B}_i$, fix $t^{in}_{i,b} = t^{out}_{i,b} = 0$. For $b \in \mathcal{B}_i$:

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r} \quad \forall i \in I, b \in \mathcal{B}_i$$

*(If no rerouting, $|R_i|=1$ and $z_{i,r}=1$ is fixed; constraints reduce to standard RECIFE form.)*

### 5.2 Timing Propagation (Running Time with Profile Selection)
For each train $i$ and section $b \in B_{i,r}$ for the selected route $r$, the exit time equals entry time plus running time (dependent on profile). Since $x_{i,p}$ is binary, we linearize using big-M:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} \rho_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \left(1 - \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r}\right)$$

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \leq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} \rho_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} + M \left(1 - \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r}\right)$$

For consecutive sections $(b, b')$ in route $r$ (where $b'$ immediately follows $b$), the entry into $b'$ equals exit from $b$:

$$t^{in}_{i,b'} = t^{out}_{i,b} \quad \forall i \in I, r \in R_i, (b, b') \in \text{seq}(B_{i,r})$$

### 5.3 Dwell Time Constraints
At scheduled stops, enforce minimum dwell:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + D^{min}_{i,b} \quad \forall i \in I, b \in S_i$$

Also enforce scheduled departure (no early departures):
$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq \tau^{dep}_{i,b} \quad \forall i \in I, b \in S_i$$

### 5.4 Release Times (Event Delays)
Trains cannot enter a section before its release time:

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq r^{min}_{i,b} \quad \forall i \in I, b \in \mathcal{B}_i$$

### 5.5 Section Capacity: Pairwise Conflicts (DTG Logic)
For each pair of trains $(i, j)$ sharing a section $b$ (i.e., $\exists r_i \in R_i, r_j \in R_j$ such that $b \in B_{i,r_i} \cap B_{j,r_j}$), ensure temporal separation. The headway $h^{DTG}_{i,p,b}$ depends on the profile of the *leading* train (braking distance to the end of authority).

**Disjunctive constraints with profile-dependent headway:**

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} \cdot x_{i,p} + h^{lock}_b \cdot \mathbb{1}_{b \in B^{sw}} - M(1 - y_{i,j,b}) - M\left(2 - \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r} - \sum_{r' \in R_j : b \in B_{j,r'}} z_{j,r'}\right)$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + \sum_{p \in P_j} h^{DTG}_{j,p,b} \cdot x_{j,p} + h^{lock}_b \cdot \mathbb{1}_{b \in B^{sw}} - M y_{i,j,b} - M\left(2 - \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r} - \sum_{r' \in R_j : b \in B_{j,r'}} z_{j,r'}\right)$$

where $\mathbb{1}_{b \in B^{sw}} = 1$ if $b$ is a switch section (0 otherwise), and the last big-M term deactivates the constraint if either train does not actually use section $b$ in its selected route.

**Linearization note:** The term $\sum_p h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} \cdot x_{i,p}$ selects the appropriate headway based on the chosen profile, maintaining linearity (no bilinear terms).

**Mutual exclusion:** For the sequencing variable to be meaningful, if both trains use the section, exactly one must lead:
$$y_{i,j,b} + y_{j,i,b} = 1 \quad \text{(if both routes include } b\text{)}$$

Or, more generally (allowing for the case where one or both skip the section):
$$y_{i,j,b} + y_{j,i,b} \leq 1$$
$$y_{i,j,b} \geq \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r} + \sum_{r' \in R_j : b \in B_{j,r'}} z_{j,r'} - 1$$
$$y_{j,i,b} \geq \sum_{r \in R_i : b \in B_{i,r}} z_{i,r} + \sum_{r' \in R_j : b \in B_{j,r'}} z_{j,r'} - 1$$

*(If routes are fixed, $y_{i,j,b} + y_{j,i,b} = 1$ holds strictly for shared sections.)*

### 5.6 Switch Section Locking (Additional Interlocking Time)
For switch sections $b \in B^{sw}$, the route-setting time $h^{lock}_b$ is already included in the headway terms above. However, if the switch must be locked for the entire passage of the leading train (from entry to clearing), the constraint is:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + h^{lock}_b - M(1 - y_{i,j,b})$$

which is subsumed by the general capacity constraint when $h^{lock}_b$ is added to the DTG headway.

### 5.7 Non-Negativity and Bounds
$$t^{in}_{i,b}, t^{out}_{i,b} \geq 0 \quad \forall i, b$$
$$d^{+}_{i,b} \geq 0 \quad \forall i, b \in S_i$$

---

## 6. Key Assumptions and Model Notes

1. **Linear Approximation of Braking Distance:** Under ETCS Level 2 DTG, the braking distance $d_{i,p}$ is calculated from the current speed to zero (or to a release speed) at the End of Authority (EOA). Since speed is continuous in reality, we discretize it into profiles $p \in P_i$ (speed classes), each associated with a pre-computed braking distance $d_{i,p}$. The mapping $h^{DTG}_{i,p,b} = \alpha_b d_{i,p} + \beta_b$ linearly approximates the blocking time from the braking curve.

2. **Brake Indication Point (BIP):** The model assumes the BIP can lie anywhere within the section, and the headway $h^{DTG}$ is conservatively computed to ensure the following train can stop before the EOA at the section exit, accounting for sighting distance, reaction time, and train length (clearing time).

3. **Big-M Selection:** The constant $M$ must be chosen carefully—larger than the maximum possible delay plus scheduling horizon (e.g., $M = 24 \times 3600$ seconds for a daily timetable) but as small as possible for computational tightness.

4. **Route-Section Coupling:** If rerouting is disabled (single route per train), variables $z_{i,r}$ are fixed to 1 for the unique route, reducing the model to the standard RECIFE-MILP structure with profile selection.

5. **Safety Margins:** All safety margins (sighting, reaction, interlocking) are assumed to be pre-calculated into the parameters $h^{DTG}$ and $h^{lock}$, ensuring the MILP remains linear while capturing the essential physics of DTG signalling.

This formulation provides a complete, linear MILP ready for implementation in solvers like CPLEX, Gurobi, or SCIP, capturing the essential trade-offs between delay minimization, speed profile optimization, and conflict resolution under modern moving-block signalling constraints.

Model 2:
# MILP Model for Conflict Detection and Resolution (CDR) under ETCS Level 2 DTG Signalling

---

## 1. Sets and Indices

| Set | Description |
|-----|-------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, indexed by $i, j$ |
| $B$ | Set of track sections (blocks), indexed by $b$ |
| $B^{SW} \subseteq B$ | Subset of **switch sections** (requiring additional interlocking/locking time) |
| $B^{PL} = B \setminus B^{SW}$ | Subset of **plain track sections** |
| $R_i$ | Set of candidate routes for train $i$, indexed by $r$ |
| $B_{i,r} \subseteq B$ | Ordered sequence of sections composing route $r$ for train $i$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of discrete speed profile options for train $i$, indexed by $p$ |
| $S_i \subseteq B$ | Set of sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop (dwell) |
| $T$ | Planning horizon: $[0, T^{max}]$ (continuous) |

**Pairs in conflict:** Let $\mathcal{C} = \{(i,j,b) : i < j \in I,\; b \in B_{i,r_i} \cap B_{j,r_j} \text{ for some } r_i \in R_i, r_j \in R_j\}$ be the set of train-pair–section combinations where a potential conflict exists.

---

## 2. Parameters

### Schedule Parameters
| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| $\tau^{arr}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at end of section $b$ (for $b \in S_i$) |
| $\tau^{dep}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled departure time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $\delta^{min}_{i,b}$ | Minimum dwell time for train $i$ at section $b \in S_i$ |
| $t^{rel}_{i,b}$ | Release time: earliest time train $i$ can enter section $b$ (accounts for initial delays) |

### Running/Blocking Time Parameters (profile-dependent)
| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| $\rho_{i,b,p}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$ |
| $L_i$ | Physical length of train $i$ |
| $d_{i,p}$ | Braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ (depends on entry speed and deceleration) |
| $d^{sight}$ | Sighting/reaction distance (constant, DTG-specific) |
| $t^{clear}_{i,b}$ | Time for train $i$ to physically clear section $b$ (tail end exits) |
| $t^{IL}_{b}$ | Interlocking/route-setting time for section $b$ |
| $t^{lock}_{b}$ | Additional locking time for switch section $b \in B^{SW}$ |

### Derived Blocking/Separation Time (DTG headway)
The DTG headway for train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$ is:

$$h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} = \frac{d_{i,p} + d^{sight} + L_i}{v^{entry}_{i,b,p}} + t^{clear}_{i,b} + t^{IL}_{b} + \begin{cases} t^{lock}_{b} & \text{if } b \in B^{SW} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

where $v^{entry}_{i,b,p}$ is the entry speed of train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$. This is **precomputed** as a parameter since $d_{i,p}$, $v^{entry}_{i,b,p}$, and all times are known constants per profile. The braking distance is approximated **linearly through the discrete speed profiles** (each profile maps to a fixed speed class, and braking distance is precomputed for that class).

### Objective Weights
| Parameter | Description |
|-----------|-------------|
| $w_i$ | Weight (priority) of train $i$'s delay |
| $\epsilon$ | Small penalty weight for profile change (deviation from default profile) |
| $M$ | Big-M constant (sufficiently large, e.g., $M = T^{max} + \max h^{DTG}$) |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| $x_{i,p}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $= 1$ if train $i$ uses speed profile $p \in P_i$ |
| $z_{i,r}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $= 1$ if train $i$ is assigned to route $r \in R_i$ |
| $t^{in}_{i,b}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Time train $i$ enters section $b$ |
| $t^{out}_{i,b}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Time train $i$ exits section $b$ |
| $y_{i,j,b}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | $= 1$ if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on section $b$; $= 0$ if $j$ precedes $i$ |
| $D_i$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$ | Positive deviation (delay) of train $i$ from its scheduled arrival at its final section |

**Note on $t^{in}_{i,b}, t^{out}_{i,b}$:** These variables are defined for all $(i,b)$ pairs where $b$ belongs to at least one candidate route of train $i$. If train $i$ does not traverse section $b$ under the chosen route, constraints ensure these variables are unconstrained (or forced to zero via indicator constraints).

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$\min \quad \sum_{i \in I} w_i \cdot D_i \;+\; \epsilon \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{chg}_{i,p} \cdot x_{i,p}$$

where $c^{chg}_{i,p} = 0$ if $p$ is the default (planned) profile for train $i$, and $c^{chg}_{i,p} = 1$ otherwise.

**Explanation:**
- **First term:** Minimizes total weighted delay (positive deviation from scheduled arrival at the destination).
- **Second term:** Small penalty encouraging the solver to keep default speed profiles unless a change reduces delay.

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Profile Selection (Exactly One Per Train)

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{1}$$

Each train must select exactly one speed profile.

---

### 5.2 Route Selection (Exactly One Per Train)

$$\sum_{r \in R_i} z_{i,r} = 1 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{2}$$

Each train must be assigned exactly one route.

---

### 5.3 Running Time Propagation Along Route

For each train $i \in I$, for each pair of consecutive sections $(b_k, b_{k+1})$ in route $r$ (i.e., $b_{k+1}$ follows $b_k$ in $B_{i,r}$):

**Entry into next section = exit from current section** (when route $r$ is selected):

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} \geq t^{out}_{i,b_k} - M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; (b_k, b_{k+1}) \in B_{i,r} \tag{3a}$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} \leq t^{out}_{i,b_k} + M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; (b_k, b_{k+1}) \in B_{i,r} \tag{3b}$$

When $z_{i,r} = 1$, these force $t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} = t^{out}_{i,b_k}$.

**Exit time = entry time + running time** (dependent on selected profile via big-M):

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \rho_{i,b,p} - M(1 - x_{i,p}) - M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; b \in B_{i,r},\; p \in P_i \tag{4a}$$

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \leq t^{in}_{i,b} + \rho_{i,b,p} + M(1 - x_{i,p}) + M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; b \in B_{i,r},\; p \in P_i \tag{4b}$$

When $x_{i,p} = 1$ and $z_{i,r} = 1$, these force $t^{out}_{i,b} = t^{in}_{i,b} + \rho_{i,b,p}$.

---

### 5.4 Minimum Dwell Time at Scheduled Stops

For each train $i \in I$ and each stop section $b \in S_i$ that belongs to route $r$:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \delta^{min}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} \rho_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; b \in S_i \cap B_{i,r},\; r \in R_i \tag{5}$$

**Note:** At stop sections, the exit time is at least the entry time plus the running time on the section plus the minimum dwell time. Since $\sum_p \rho_{i,b,p} x_{i,p}$ is the selected running time (exactly one $x_{i,p} = 1$), this is a linear expression. Alternatively, constraints (4a)–(4b) can be relaxed at stops and replaced by:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \delta^{min}_{i,b} + \rho_{i,b,p} - M(1 - x_{i,p}) - M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i,\; b \in S_i \cap B_{i,r},\; p,\; r \tag{5'}$$

with no upper bound (allowing longer dwells).

---

### 5.5 Release Times (Earliest Entry)

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{rel}_{i,b} \cdot z_{i,r} \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; b \in B_{i,r} \tag{6}$$

Train $i$ cannot enter section $b$ before its release time (accounts for delayed departures from origin, connections, etc.). When $z_{i,r} = 0$, the constraint is non-binding.

---

### 5.6 Section Capacity — DTG Pairwise Disjunctive Constraints

For each pair $(i,j,b) \in \mathcal{C}$ (i.e., trains $i \neq j$ both potentially using section $b$), and for each combination of profiles $p \in P_i$, $q \in P_j$:

**If $i$ precedes $j$ on section $b$ ($y_{i,j,b} = 1$):**

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} - M(1 - y_{i,j,b}) - M(1 - x_{i,p}) - M(1 - z_{i,r_i}) - M(1 - z_{j,r_j}) \tag{7a}$$

$$\forall (i,j,b) \in \mathcal{C},\; p \in P_i,\; r_i \ni b,\; r_j \ni b$$

**If $j$ precedes $i$ on section $b$ ($y_{i,j,b} = 0$):**

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + h^{DTG}_{j,b,q} - M \cdot y_{i,j,b} - M(1 - x_{j,q}) - M(1 - z_{i,r_i}) - M(1 - z_{j,r_j}) \tag{7b}$$

$$\forall (i,j,b) \in \mathcal{C},\; q \in P_j,\; r_i \ni b,\; r_j \ni b$$

**Explanation:**
- When $y_{i,j,b} = 1$, $x_{i,p} = 1$, and both routes are selected: constraint (7a) enforces that train $j$ cannot enter section $b$ until train $i$ has exited **plus** the DTG headway $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$, which accounts for:
  - Braking distance $d_{i,p}$ (speed-dependent, via profile $p$)
  - Sighting/reaction distance
  - Train length clearance
  - Interlocking time
  - Additional switch locking time (if $b \in B^{SW}$)
- When $y_{i,j,b} = 0$: constraint (7b) is the symmetric case with $j$ preceding $i$.
- The binary variable $y_{i,j,b}$ selects which disjunct is active.
- Constraints are deactivated via big-M when either train's route does not include $b$.

---

### 5.7 Switch Section Additional Locking

For switch sections $b \in B^{SW}$, the interlocking must be set and locked before the first train enters, and the lock must be held until the train clears. This is captured by the extended headway $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ (already includes $t^{lock}_b$). Additionally, for a switch section shared by multiple routes, the route-setting constraint:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + t^{lock}_b - M(1 - y_{i,j,b}) - M(1 - z_{i,r_i}) - M(1 - z_{j,r_j}) \tag{8}$$

$$\forall (i,j,b) \in \mathcal{C},\; b \in B^{SW},\; r_i \ni b,\; r_j \ni b,\; r_i \neq r_j \text{ (different switch positions)}$$

This ensures that when a switch section must be re-locked for a different route, an additional locking time is imposed.

---

### 5.8 Delay Definition (Positive Deviation from Schedule)

For each train $i$, let $b^{last}_i$ denote the final section of its route (destination). Since the route is selected, we define:

$$D_i \geq t^{out}_{i,b^{last}_i} - \tau^{arr}_{i,b^{last}_i} - M(1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall i \in I,\; r \in R_i,\; b^{last}_i = \text{last}(B_{i,r}) \tag{9a}$$

$$D_i \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in I \tag{9b}$$

$D_i$ captures the positive deviation (delay) from the scheduled arrival time. Early arrivals are not penalized.

---

### 5.9 Time Bounds

$$0 \leq t^{in}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall i, b \tag{10a}$$

$$0 \leq t^{out}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall i, b \tag{10b}$$

---

## 6. Complete MILP Formulation Summary

$$\min \quad \sum_{i \in I} w_i D_i + \epsilon \sum_{i \in I} \sum_{p \in P_i} c^{chg}_{i,p} x_{i,p}$$

**subject to:**

| Constraint | Equation | Description |
|-----------|----------|-------------|
| Profile selection | (1) | One speed profile per train |
| Route selection | (2) | One route per train |
| Temporal propagation | (3a)–(3b) | Consecutive section timing |
| Running time | (4a)–(4b) | Exit = entry + profile-dependent running time |
| Dwell time | (5) or (5′) | Minimum dwell at stops |
| Release times | (6) | Earliest section entry |
| Section capacity (DTG) | (7a)–(7b) | Pairwise disjunctive headway with speed-dependent separation |
| Switch locking | (8) | Additional locking for switch reconfiguration |
| Delay definition | (9a)–(9b) | Positive deviation from schedule |
| Time bounds | (10a)–(10b) | Planning horizon limits |

**Variable domains:**
- $x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall i \in I, p \in P_i$
- $z_{i,r} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall i \in I, r \in R_i$
- $y_{i,j,b} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall (i,j,b) \in \mathcal{C}$
- $t^{in}_{i,b}, t^{out}_{i,b} \in [0, T^{max}] \quad \forall i, b$
- $D_i \geq 0 \quad \forall i \in I$

---

## 7. Assumptions and Modeling Notes

### 7.1 Linear Approximation of Braking Distance
The braking distance $d_{i,p}$ is **not** modeled as a nonlinear function of speed. Instead, each speed profile $p \in P_i$ corresponds to a **discrete speed class** (e.g., 60 km/h, 80 km/h, 100 km/h, 120 km/h), and the braking distance is **precomputed** for each class using the standard formula $d = v^2 / (2a)$ or railway-specific braking curves. The headway $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ is then a **fixed parameter** per (train, section, profile) triple, maintaining linearity.

### 7.2 DTG Signalling Specifics
Under ETCS Level 2 with Distance-to-Go (DTG):
- The **End of Authority (EOA)** is at the end of the occupied section ahead.
- The **brake indication point** can lie anywhere along the train's path (not fixed at block boundaries), which is why the headway depends on the **braking distance of the following train** rather than fixed block boundaries.
- The model captures this by making the separation constraint (7a)–(7b) depend on $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$, which incorporates $d_{i,p}$, the sighting distance, and the train length.

### 7.3 Big-M Tightening
The big-M constant should be calibrated per constraint for computational efficiency:
- For timing constraints: $M = T^{max}$ suffices.
- For capacity constraints: $M = T^{max} + \max_{i,b,p} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ suffices.
- Tighter, constraint-specific $M$ values significantly improve LP relaxation bounds and solver performance.

### 7.4 Deterministic Model
This is a deterministic model assuming all parameters (running times, braking distances, scheduled times) are known with certainty. For robustness under uncertainty, stochastic programming or robust optimization extensions would be needed.

### 7.5 Scalability
The pairwise conflict constraints (7a)–(7b) grow as $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B| \cdot |P|^2)$ in the worst case. Preprocessing to identify only truly conflicting pairs (trains whose time windows overlap on shared sections) is essential for practical instances.

### 7.6 RECIFE-MILP Extension
This model extends the RECIFE-MILP framework (originally developed for fixed-block signalling) by:
- Introducing **speed-profile-dependent headways** ($h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ varies with $p$, unlike fixed-block where headway is constant per section).
- Adding **profile selection variables** $x_{i,p}$ and their coupling with both timing and capacity constraints.
- Incorporating **DTG-specific parameters** (braking distance, sighting distance, EOA location) into the headway calculation.
- Handling **switch sections** with additional interlocking/locking constraints.

Model 3:
# Conflict Detection and Resolution MILP for Railway Traffic Management under ETCS Level 2 DTG Signalling

## 1. Complete Model Formulation

### 1.1 Sets and Indices

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $I$ | Set of trains, $i \in I$ |
| $B$ | Set of all track sections (blocks), $b \in B$ |
| $B^{SW} \subset B$ | Subset of **switch sections** (require additional locking time) |
| $B^{PL} = B \setminus B^{SW}$ | Subset of plain track sections |
| $B^{stop}_i \subseteq R_i$ | Sections where train $i$ has a scheduled stop |
| $R_i$ | Set of alternative routes for train $i$, $r \in R_i$ |
| $R_i(r) = (b_{i,r,1}, b_{i,r,2}, \ldots, b_{i,r,n_{i,r}})$ | Ordered sequence of sections for route $r$ of train $i$ |
| $P_i$ | Set of speed profile options for train $i$, $p \in P_i$ |
| $S$ | Set of discrete event time indices (for possible discretization of releases) |

For the remainder, when a single route is considered (or after route selection), we denote by $(b_{i,1}, b_{i,2}, \ldots, b_{i,n_i})$ the sequence of sections along the selected route of train $i$. We write $b \prec_i b'$ when $b$ immediately precedes $b'$ in the route of train $i$.

### 1.2 Parameters

| Symbol | Definition |
|--------|------------|
| $\tau^{A}_{i}$ | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at its final destination |
| $\tau^{A}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled arrival time of train $i$ at section $b$ (if applicable) |
| $\tau^{D}_{i,b}$ | Scheduled departure time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $\delta^{min}_{i,b}$ | Minimum dwell time of train $i$ at stop section $b \in B^{stop}_i$ |
| $rt_{i,b,p}$ | Running time of train $i$ on section $b$ under speed profile $p$ |
| $bt_{i,b,p}$ | Blocking (occupation) time of section $b$ by train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $d_{i,p}$ | Braking distance of train $i$ under profile $p$ (speed-dependent) |
| $d^{sight}_{i,p}$ | Sighting/reaction distance for train $i$ under profile $p$ |
| $d^{sight+brake}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$ | Total DTG approach distance |
| $t^{clear}_{i}$ | Clearing time (time for full train to vacate a section after entry) |
| $t^{route}_{b}$ | Interlocking/route-setting time for section $b$ |
| $t^{lock}_{b}$ | Additional locking time for switch section $b \in B^{SW}$ |
| $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ | DTG separation headway: minimum time interval that train $i$ under profile $p$ must allow before another train can enter section $b$ (see §2.3) |
| $t^{rel}_{i,b}$ | Release time (earliest possible entry) of train $i$ at section $b$ |
| $w_i$ | Weight (priority) of train $i$ in the objective |
| $\lambda$ | Small penalty coefficient for profile changes (profile deviating from nominal) |
| $p^{nom}_i$ | Nominal (default) speed profile for train $i$ |
| $M$ | Big-M constant (sufficiently large positive number) |
| $T^{max}$ | Time horizon upper bound |
| $T^{min}$ | Time horizon lower bound |

### 1.3 Decision Variables

| Variable | Type | Domain | Definition |
|----------|------|--------|------------|
| $x_{i,p}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ uses speed profile $p$ |
| $z_{i,r}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ uses route $r \in R_i$ |
| $t^{in}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $[T^{min}, T^{max}]$ | Entry time of train $i$ into section $b$ |
| $t^{out}_{i,b}$ | Continuous | $[T^{min}, T^{max}]$ | Exit time of train $i$ from section $b$ |
| $y_{i,j,b}$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ precedes train $j$ on shared section $b$ |
| $d_i$ | Continuous | $\geq 0$ | Positive deviation (delay) of train $i$ at final destination |
| $u_i$ | Binary | $\{0,1\}$ | $=1$ if train $i$ deviates from nominal profile (used for penalty) |

---

### 1.4 Objective Function

$$\min \; \sum_{i \in I} w_i \cdot d_i \; + \; \lambda \sum_{i \in I} u_i$$

**Interpretation:** Minimize total weighted positive deviation from scheduled arrival times at final destinations, plus a small penalty for speed profile changes relative to nominal profiles (encouraging solution stability).

---

### 1.5 Constraints

#### (C1) Exactly One Speed Profile per Train

$$\sum_{p \in P_i} x_{i,p} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one speed profile.

---

#### (C2) Exactly One Route per Train

$$\sum_{r \in R_i} z_{i,r} = 1 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

Each train must select exactly one route from its set of alternatives.

---

#### (C3) Profile Deviation Indicator

$$u_i \geq 1 - x_{i,p^{nom}_i} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

If the nominal profile is not selected ($x_{i,p^{nom}_i} = 0$), then $u_i = 1$ and the penalty is incurred. Since we minimize, $u_i$ will be pushed to $0$ when possible.

---

#### (C4) Timing Propagation Along Route — Running Time (Big-M Linearization over Profiles)

For each train $i \in I$ and each pair of consecutive sections $(b_k, b_{k+1})$ along its route sequence:

$$t^{out}_{i,b_k} \geq t^{in}_{i,b_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b_k,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; \forall \, b_k \in \text{route of } i$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} = t^{out}_{i,b_k} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; b_{k+1} \text{ follows } b_k \text{ in route of } i$$

**Note:** The running time constraint uses the linear expression $\sum_p rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p}$ which selects the correct running time via the profile binary. This is already linear (no additional big-M needed) because $x_{i,p}$ multiplies a constant parameter $rt_{i,b,p}$, producing a bilinear term that is linear since $x_{i,p} \in \{0,1\}$.

More precisely, the constraint is:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; \forall \, b \text{ on route of } i$$

When route selection binaries $z_{i,r}$ are active, we additionally enforce that times are only constrained for sections on the selected route:

$$t^{out}_{i,b} \geq t^{in}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall \, i, r \in R_i, b \in R_i(r)$$

---

#### (C5) Minimum Dwell Time at Scheduled Stops

$$t^{out}_{i,b} - t^{in}_{i,b} \geq \delta^{min}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; b \in B^{stop}_i$$

At stop sections, the total occupancy (entry to exit) must be at least the running time plus the minimum dwell time.

---

#### (C6) Release Times (Earliest Entry)

$$t^{in}_{i,b_{i,1}} \geq t^{rel}_{i,b_{i,1}} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

The first section entry for each train cannot precede its release time (which may account for upstream delays or scheduled departure).

---

#### (C7) Section Capacity / Conflict Resolution — DTG Separation

For each pair of trains $(i, j)$, $i \neq j$, sharing a section $b \in B$:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - y_{i,j,b})$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + \sum_{p \in P_j} h^{DTG}_{j,b,p} \cdot x_{j,p} - M \cdot y_{i,j,b}$$

$$\forall \, (i,j) \in I \times I, \; i \neq j, \; \forall \, b \in B: b \in R_i \cap R_j$$

**Semantics of $y_{i,j,b}$:** When $y_{i,j,b} = 1$, train $i$ goes first on section $b$ and the first constraint becomes active (forcing $j$ to wait until $i$ clears plus the DTG headway). When $y_{i,j,b} = 0$, the second constraint becomes active (forcing $i$ to wait for $j$).

---

#### (C8) DTG Headway Definition (Speed-Dependent Separation)

The DTG headway parameter $h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$ is computed offline as:

$$h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} = \frac{d^{sight+brake}_{i,p}}{v_{i,p,b}} + t^{clear}_i + t^{route}_b$$

where:
- $v_{i,p,b}$ is the speed of train $i$ on section $b$ under profile $p$ (parameter),
- $d^{sight+brake}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$ is the total distance the driver/system needs from the brake indication point to the End of Authority (EoA),
- $t^{clear}_i$ is the clearing time for the train to fully exit,
- $t^{route}_b$ is the interlocking route-setting time.

**Key DTG modelling assumption:** Under ETCS Level 2 DTG, the brake indication point can lie anywhere along the track (not just at block boundaries). The End of Authority is the section end. Thus, the minimum separation time for a following train is determined by the time for the leading train to travel the sighting + braking distance at its current speed, plus clearing and route-setting margins.

---

#### (C9) Switch Section Additional Locking

For switch sections $b \in B^{SW}$, the separation constraints are augmented:

$$t^{in}_{j,b} \geq t^{out}_{i,b} + \sum_{p \in P_i} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} \cdot x_{i,p} + t^{lock}_b - M \cdot (1 - y_{i,j,b})$$

$$t^{in}_{i,b} \geq t^{out}_{j,b} + \sum_{p \in P_j} h^{DTG}_{j,b,p} \cdot x_{j,p} + t^{lock}_b - M \cdot y_{i,j,b}$$

$$\forall \, (i,j), \; i \neq j, \; \forall \, b \in B^{SW}: b \in R_i \cap R_j$$

The additional $t^{lock}_b$ accounts for the longer interlocking locking time required when a switch (turnout) is involved.

---

#### (C10) Delay Computation (Positive Deviation from Scheduled Arrival)

$$d_i \geq t^{in}_{i,b^{final}_i} - \tau^{A}_{i} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

$$d_i \geq 0 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

The delay variable $d_i$ captures only the **positive** deviation (tardiness) from the scheduled arrival time at the final section.

---

#### (C11) Route Consistency (Optional Rerouting)

When multiple routes are available, constraints (C4) and (C7)–(C9) are only enforced for sections on the selected route. This is achieved by conditioning with $z_{i,r}$:

For timing propagation on route $r$:
$$t^{out}_{i,b_k} \geq t^{in}_{i,b_k} + \sum_{p \in P_i} rt_{i,b_k,p} \cdot x_{i,p} - M \cdot (1 - z_{i,r}) \quad \forall \, i, r \in R_i, \; b_k \in R_i(r)$$

For conflict resolution, only pairs $(i,j)$ whose selected routes share section $b$ need constraints. This can be enforced by:

$$y_{i,j,b} \leq \sum_{r \in R_i: \, b \in R_i(r)} z_{i,r} \quad \forall \, i, j, b$$

$$y_{i,j,b} \leq \sum_{r \in R_j: \, b \in R_j(r)} z_{i,r} \quad \forall \, i, j, b$$

(These ensure $y_{i,j,b}$ is only meaningful when both trains actually traverse $b$.)

Alternatively, the conflict constraints can be relaxed with an additional $-M(2 - z_{i,r} - z_{j,r'})$ term when both routes must include $b$.

---

#### (C12) Binary and Continuous Variable Bounds

$$x_{i,p} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; p \in P_i$$

$$z_{i,r} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I, \; r \in R_i$$

$$y_{i,j,b} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, (i,j), b$$

$$u_i \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

$$T^{min} \leq t^{in}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall \, i, b$$

$$T^{min} \leq t^{out}_{i,b} \leq T^{max} \quad \forall \, i, b$$

$$d_i \geq 0 \quad \forall \, i \in I$$

---

## 2. Explanation of Model Elements

### 2.1 Speed Profile Selection (C1, C3)

Each train selects exactly one speed profile from its feasible set $P_i$. A speed profile defines a complete speed trajectory: running times $rt_{i,b,p}$ on each section and associated braking distances $d_{i,p}$. This is the mechanism by which different speed classes (e.g., line speed vs. reduced speed) affect both running time and the DTG separation headway. The penalty variable $u_i$ and coefficient $\lambda$ discourage unnecessary deviations from the nominal profile, promoting solution stability and driver comfort.

### 2.2 Timing Propagation (C4, C5, C6)

Train movement along its route is modelled as a sequence of section entries and exits. The entry into the next section equals the exit from the previous one ($t^{in}_{i,b_{k+1}} = t^{out}_{i,b_k}$). The exit time from a section is the entry time plus the running time, which depends on the selected speed profile. At scheduled stops, an additional minimum dwell time is imposed. Release times prevent trains from starting before they are physically or operationally ready.

### 2.3 DTG Headway Derivation (C8)

This is the core ETCS Level 2 DTG-specific element. Under DTG signalling:
- There are **no fixed block signals**; the movement authority extends continuously to the end of the authority (section end).
- The brake indication point (BIP) is the location where the train must begin braking to stop before the EoA. It can lie **anywhere** along the track.
- The minimum separation between two trains on the same section is the time needed for the leading train to travel from the BIP to the EoA, plus clearing and interlocking margins.

The separation distance is:
$$d^{sep}_{i,p} = d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}$$

This is the sum of the **sighting/reaction distance** (distance travelled during the driver's/system's reaction time before braking commences) and the **braking distance** (distance to come to a stop or reach the target speed).

The headway time is then:
$$h^{DTG}_{i,b,p} = \frac{d^{sight}_{i,p} + d_{i,p}}{v_{i,p,b}} + t^{clear}_i + t^{route}_b$$

The division by speed converts the spatial separation to a temporal one. Since different profiles $p$ imply different speeds $v_{i,p,b}$ and different braking distances $d_{i,p}$, the headway is profile-dependent and is activated via the $x_{i,p}$ binaries.

### 2.4 Conflict Resolution (C7, C9)

The pairwise disjunctive (big-M) constraints with binary variables $y_{i,j,b}$ resolve conflicts on shared sections. For any two trains sharing a section:
- Either train $i$ precedes $j$ (when $y_{i,j,b} = 1$): train $j$ cannot enter until train $i$ has exited plus the DTG headway.
- Or train $j$ precedes $i$ (when $y_{i,j,b} = 0$): symmetric constraint.

For **switch sections**, the additional locking time $t^{lock}_b$ is added to both constraints. This reflects the operational reality that switches require longer interlocking locking before the route can be set for the next train (due to mechanical locking, flank protection, and overlap release).

### 2.5 Objective Function

The objective minimizes:
1. **Total weighted delay**: $\sum_i w_i \cdot d_i$ where $d_i$ is the positive deviation from the scheduled arrival time at the train's destination. Higher-priority trains (e.g., high-speed passenger services) receive larger weights $w_i$.
2. **Profile change penalty**: $\lambda \sum_i u_i$ where $\lambda$ is small (e.g., $0.01$). This acts as a regularization term, ensuring that speed profile changes are only used when they meaningfully reduce delay.

### 2.6 Optional Rerouting (C2, C11)

When alternative routes exist, binary variables $z_{i,r}$ select one route per train. All timing and conflict constraints are conditioned on route selection via big-M terms. This allows the model to reroute trains around conflicts when beneficial, subject to the constraint that all timing and capacity constraints are only enforced on the actually selected route.

---

## 3. Assumptions and Simplifications

### 3.1 Linearization of Braking Distance

The braking distance $d_{i,p}$ is a nonlinear function of speed (typically $d \propto v^2 / (2a)$ for constant deceleration $a$). In this MILP, we assume:

> **Assumption A1:** The continuous braking-distance-to-speed relationship is **discretized into speed classes** represented by the profiles $P_i$. Each profile $p$ corresponds to a specific speed (or speed trajectory) with a pre-computed braking distance $d_{i,p}$. This makes the separation constraints linear.

### 3.2 Deterministic Parameters

All parameters (running times, headways, scheduled times) are assumed deterministic and known. Stochastic variations (e.g., driver behaviour, weather) are not modelled.

### 3.3 Fixed Train Lengths and Clearing Times

Train lengths and clearing times are fixed parameters. The clearing time $t^{clear}_i$ already incorporates the train length divided by its speed under each profile.

### 3.4 Big-M Formulation

The disjunctive constraints use big-M. The value of $M$ must be sufficiently large (e.g., $M = T^{max} + \max_{i,b,p} h^{DTG}_{i,b,p}$) but as small as possible for computational efficiency.

### 3.5 Single-Direction Sections

Each section $b$ is used in one direction at a time. For bidirectional sections, additional constraints or separate section identifiers per direction are needed.

### 3.6 Infinite Capacity at Platforms

Platform capacity is not explicitly modelled; it is assumed that platform tracks are available when trains arrive. This can be relaxed by treating platform tracks as sections with capacity constraints.

---

## 4. Summary Table of Constraints

| Constraint | Type | Count |
|------------|------|-------|
| (C1) Profile selection | Equality | $|I|$ |
| (C2) Route selection | Equality | $|I|$ |
| (C3) Profile deviation | Inequality | $|I|$ |
| (C4) Running time | Inequality | $\sum_i |R_i|$ |
| (C5) Dwell time | Inequality | $\sum_i |B^{stop}_i|$ |
| (C6) Release time | Inequality | $|I|$ |
| (C7) Conflict (plain) | Disjunctive pair | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B|)$ |
| (C9) Conflict (switch) | Disjunctive pair | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B^{SW}|)$ |
| (C10) Delay computation | Inequality | $2|I|$ |
| (C11) Route consistency | Inequality | $O(|I|^2 \cdot |B| \cdot |R|)$ |
| (C12) Bounds | Domain | All variables |

---

## 5. Extension Notes

- **Rolling horizon**: The model can be embedded in a rolling-horizon framework where it is re-solved periodically as new information (delays, disruptions) arrives.
- **Energy-aware profiles**: The speed profiles $P_i$ can be extended to include energy-optimal trajectories, adding an energy term to the objective.
- **Robustness**: Buffer times can be added to headways $h^{DTG}$ to absorb minor perturbations.
- **Passenger connections**: Additional constraints can enforce minimum connection times for passenger transfers at stations.
